videos.title: FEM@LLNL | New Advances in hypre 3.0 for Mixed Precision and Semi-Structured Problems

segments.text: So, welcome to another edition of the Finite  Element seminar at Lawrence Livermore National
Lab. Thank you for joining us. Today it's my  pleasure to introduce Rob Falgout, who is going
to tell us about the new advances in hypre-3.0  that just came out recently. Rob got his degree
from the University of Virginia and joined the Lab  almost 35 years ago, is that right? Wow. That's
34. 34, and as you probably know him from being  the project lead for hypre, but he's done other
things. He's worked on the ParFlow project, he's  leading the efforts in parallel time integration,
the XBraid project, won a lot of awards, he's a  distinguished member of the technical staff, SIAM
fellow, and currently he's in the SIAM activity  group on supercomputing career prize awarding.
But today he's gonna go into the nitty gritty of  software in hypre, so, looking, looking forward to
that. The floor is yours. Thanks, thanks Rob for  agreeing to present. Hey, thanks Tzanio. Thanks
for the introduction and, and the invitation. So,  as Tzanio said, yeah, today's gonna be talking
about basically hypre-3.0, the new release that  came out, and I'll be focusing on the two main
additions that we made to this new release. So, I  won't tell you everything about the new release,
but I'll tell you these two, I'll go into details  about mixed precision and the semi-structured
updates, and I'll do that in reverse order I'll  start with semi-structured in the second half.
The last part of the talk will be about mixed  precision. So, here are the team members. What
I'm gonna present today was not just done by  me, obviously, it was done by the whole team,
and they deserve a lot of credit. Okay, I won't  tell you what multigrid is, but just a reminder
about hypre, one of the main things we focus on is  developing multigrid methods. So, that's the main,
one of the main features of the library. The  reason is because we're interested in solving
really large problems and they have this O(N)  scalability potential. There are many algorithms,
I'll describe a couple today as I go through  the new features and yeah, okay, another unique
feature of, the hypre library is these linear  system interfaces. We call them conceptual
linear system interfaces, and this little diagram  sort of illustrates how it works. Across the top,
we've got the interfaces themselves and they're  just ways of describing your linear system to the
code. So, on the right, for example, is the  standard linear algebra way where you'd say,
row I comma J column, column J has coefficient  blah. All the way on the left is what I would call
a structured interface. Here you might have grids,  structured grids, and you describe your linear
system in terms of stencils, and then in between  there's is what we call semi-structure. So,
I'll be talking a lot about this, this left part  today. The reason this is useful is because if you
provide extra information about structure, then  you can store things differently and something
that's more native and, and takes advantage of  structure and write algorithms that also take
advantage of structure. At the same time, because  this is just an interface, we could build a more
unstructured structured data structure under the  hood and, and use them a more general method such
as algebraic multigrid. And that just, you know,  you still have the same interface for describing
a linear system, you just switch a couple,  flip a couple of knobs and you get a different
storage object type, as we call it, out and then  you can use different solvers. An example of a
semi-structured grid is kind of shown here  this in this, it's a block structured thing.
You can see each one of these five parts has  structure in it in the, the normal cartesian way,
and you can describe the couplings within a part  in terms of stencils. And then, of course, because
these things are coupled together, you have to do  something between the part boundaries, and that's
why it's semi-structured not just structured,  and I'll say more about that in the next slide,
several slides. Okay, so I'll start with what we  had in hypre before hypre-3.0 and we had three
main sort of underlying data storage objects  or matrix objects. One was a struct matrix,
and this image on the right is for, for the struct  matrix, and it was it's composed out of what we
call a grid, and for us a grid is a union of boxes  on a cartesian index space, so a box is described
by its lower and upper corner. And then on top of  that grid, you have a stencil, which is a non-zero
pattern basically for your operator and for the  row of your operator that describes how data on
this grid is coupled to its neighbors. And then  of course along with this stencil, which is just
giving you some structured information, you need  the actual data itself. So, we have an array of
data, and that can vary across the grid, so the  stencil is not constant coefficient. It wouldn't
necessarily be like a 4 minus 1 five-point  stencil everywhere, those coefficients can vary,
but they can also be constant in the code. We  have a way of storing much less data and then
designing our algorithms to, to use that data in  an efficient way. So, that's the structured part
of the structured matrix. We also have a general  compressed sparse row matrix, parallel compressed
sparse row matrix, which is composed out of two  serial compressed sparse row matrix, one for the
diagonal block that couples state unknowns on the  processor with itself and then the off-diagonal
part couples to couples to off-diagonal data. And  then the semi-structured matrix is a combination
of the two. So, semi-structured grids can look  like the things on the right. I showed you the
block structured one already. You can have  structured adaptive mesh refinement as well
and things like overset grids. So, you can be  pretty complicated scenarios that you have. Okay,
so one of the reasons for this release is that  previously, we had some limitations in what we
could do in the semi-structured code. So, both,  I'll start at the top here and here's a picture
from the previous slide. And we had for both  structured and semi-structured matrices, we had,
we required that they had to be a square in the  previous code. And so that meant that, well,
and this is just a reminder of how this works, you  know, struct matrix, as I just said, is a stencil
applied to a single grid, and the semi-struct  is a combination, in fact it's a sum of matrices
of a structured type and then unstructured with  the ParCSR. But because things had to be square,
the matrix-vector multiply was only for square  matrices, and we also didn't even have a general
matrix-matrix multiply routine in the code.  And of course, these kinds of matrix-vector and
matrix-matrix type kernels are really important  for designing and, and implementing solvers. So,
this is limited what we could do in the in the  code before. Now we did have multigrid solvers in
the first in the structured grid case. Two of them  are listed here, SMG is Schaffer multigrid, it's
not actually semi-coarsening multigrid, and PFMG,  but they are both semi-coarsening methods. If this
is your grid, you take every other point in one  direction and that gives you a semi-coarsening
pattern. One of them is very robust. SMG  is very robust, but it's very expensive,
and the other is a little less robust, but it's  much more efficient, and I'll say more about PFMG,
it'll come up again in a later context. But in  order to implement this, interpret things like
interpolation and restriction which correspond  to multiplication of rectangular matrices,
had to be implemented by hand, and they were also  hard-coded for very specific stencil cases. So,
it wasn't very general code. It was, it  was written specifically for these solvers,
and it made it difficult to experiment with and,  and extend the solvers to do different things, and
in particular it made it difficult to implement  multigrid solvers in the semi-structured case. So,
this semi-structured idea came about and was even  implemented in like the early 2000s, 2002-2003
timeframe. And we had the idea of, of writing  multigrid methods that were semi-structured
multigrid methods way back when, but we didn't  have the tools to do it, so it kind of sat around
as an idea for a very long time. And what we had  up until just recently was very limited, support,
we didn't really have multigrid methods. We had  something where you basically use this splitting
up here and you could apply SMG or PFMG to, to  this part of the problem and, and, and have an
iterative method that's sort of built in that,  that way. So anyway, this motivates what we did
with the overhaul of the semi-structured code in  hypre-3.0, and this is sort of an outline of what
we did. Basically, we extended the matrix-vector  class beyond just using square matrices. So,
you know, the Matvec does rectangular matrices  as well. The implementation, implementation still
supports both variable and constant-coefficients  in the matrix and combinations thereof. We still
based on stencils, but now we have to change what  it means to be a stencil. This was a big partof
this implementation is how do we even define what  it means to be a, a stencil-based rectangular
matrix? And there are advantages of this. I've  already alluded to a lot of these. It simplifies
implementation. You can reuse a lot of kernels,  and code optimization can also be isolated to a
few kernels, but it also makes it trickier because  these are now general kernels as opposed to very
specific ones that were written for individual  algorithms. And then we can extend this now to
implement methods in the semi-structured case,  and I'll show I'll tell you a little bit about a
new solver that's also available in the release  for the first time, this semi-structured AMG
algorithm. Just historically a little bit, the  redesign that is now in hypre-3.0, it really
started more than a decade ago and we've been  working sort of on and off on it. So, it's we've,
it's been a long process to say that least, but  it's nice that it's actually in the code and,
and being used in useful, useful ways now. Another  point I wanted to make in case you had noticed is
that this is the first major release we've done in  almost 19 years, so we had hypre-2.-something for
a really long time until just this past September.  Okay, so that's kind of an overview. Now what I'm
gonna do is dive into the details a little more  about what happened and, and what we did. So,
starting with extending to rectangular matrices,  okay? So, basically I mentioned this already,
now a matrix has both the domain and a range grid,  so it has two different grids, one it, it computes
on and one it maps to, to put the result. And we  had a bunch of different iterations in this as we
were writing the code and what, what we ended  up in the, in the end was defining this domain
in range grid in terms of a common base grid.  So, basically each one of these grids here is
a coarsening of some common base grid, okay? And  that ended up being very useful to do. So, this,
now when you have a stencil, you have to think  about which index space it, it actually operates
on, that'll become more clear when I do the  example down at the below. So, there's, there's
a concept of a stencil grid. Right now, it's one  of these two, the domain or the range, whichever
one is the finer of the two. But we'll probably be  generalizing that in, in the future for a variety
of reasons. And then we have another restriction  about how these matrices can be defined,
these stencil-based matrices can be defined and  it's, we have to be able to represent the stencil
in a compact way, I call it a range stencil here,  which is really hard to explain, but you'll get a
sense for what I mean down here in the example.  So, let's do this example real quick, thinking
about interpolation in this PFMG algorithm. So,  let's look at the pictures first, on the left is
a fine grid, and, and if we semi-coarsen in just  the X direction, the darker bands here would be,
would correspond to what the coarse grid is, so  I get this coarse grid based on that coarsening
pattern, and then the way we do interpolation in  PFMG is just two-point interpolation. So, if by,
by doing this coarsening, we've, this is AMG  terminology, we've now separated the points and
the fine grid into two different types of sets,  we normally call them C points and F points. So,
the C points are the dark regions here and the  F points of the light regions, so if I'm at an
F point to do interpolation like at the 3,3 point,  I take some sort of combination of values from the
left and the right, and I put the result here  on the fine grid at 3,3. If however, I am at
a C point on the fine grid, then I just multiply  the coarse grid value by 1 and then and, and put
it on the fine grid at the C point location. So as  from a notation wise, we can represent this as two
stencils here in second line here. The left one  is when we apply the stencil and put the result
at a fine point on the range grid, and the right  one is when we apply a stencil and put it at the,
a coarse point in the range grid. And the reason  I've written it as two different stencils here
‘cause these are more like what you would normally  have in the stencil. Everywhere there's an
asterisk here, there's no coefficient, so this  is a two-point stencil. It represents a row in
the matrix P that only has two coefficients in it,  two non-zero coefficients in it. And then second
stencil again it only has one non-zero coefficient  in this case and it's always a 1 in this case, and
it represents those rows in in interpolation that  only have a single 1 in them. So, P is really a
sum of these two more standard stencils, and what  we meant up here by one of the limitations about
either you have to store the matrix itself as a  single range stencil or its transpose. In this
particular case for interpolation, if you write  its transpose, you only get one of these stencils,
you only need one stencil to explain it in this  decomposition here, and that's important for the
way we store things and do things internally in  the code. Okay, and just another a note real quick
before I move on to the next slide, this is a  stencil here on the right for the coarse grid
operator, and I've, for a coarse grid operator,  here it's nine point, and that would be applied
on this coarse grid, okay? So, the, this first  slide will be about Matvec and the next two will
be about matrix-matrix multiply. So, one of the  things in the Matvec that we've also done is,
we've always had a notion of ghost zones in hypre,  and this is an extra layer of, of space in the
data structure where you can put information from  neighboring processors in a communication phase
and so that you can then do your computations  really efficiently locally. But deciding how
many ghost layers you need a priori, which is  what we had to do in the previous implementation,
is quite difficult because it really depends on  the algorithm and algorithms internally that are
gonna be used and what they do. So, here's kind of  a simple example of something that happens in just
a multigrid method. It's all in 1D here, so in the  blue box above, think of this as just a piece of
an index space on the fine grid and we've got  some boxes here that described the data on
this processor that lives on this processor  for a vector X on the fine grid, okay? And,
no, actually it's not a vector X that lives on  the fine grid. This is just, this is just for a
vector on the fine grid. And when the coarse grid  is in, you take every other grid point and then
and you end up with some boxes, some of them drop  out, like this 35 disappears entirely when you
coarsen, and so you have this grid here. Okay, so  now let's think about multiplying interpolation
time this vector X now, think about it living on  the coarse grid. So, we have two different kinds
of operations we might wanna do. We might  want to multiply it by interpolation to map
information to a fine grid or we might multiply by  the coarse grid operator itself and where it just
stays on the coarse grid. And so to do that, you  need to add some ghost zones, and that's what this
lighter region is sort of indicating. In the  case of multiplying P times X, you, your data
space with the extra ghost zones looks like this.  So, you still have six boxes, but they aren't,
they're a little bit larger than the ones we start  out with on the fine grid. And for multiplying
by AC, you again, we have to do the same, same  thing, it's a little more clear here. You know,
look at this box here, I've added a ghost zone to  the left and the right and that's kind of typical
for a three-point stencil, so you have one ghost  zone to the left and the right. But the, the,
the main thing to notice here is we're operating  on the same vector X, and the data space for that
vector looks different. Here you've got six boxes  with of different sizes and here you've got four,
and so if you want to prevent when you're doing  P times X and, and then multiplying later times
the coarse grid, if you want to prevent doing a  bunch of copies and resizing of data, you kind of
have to take a union of these two ideas together  and store, store X so that it can support both
types of operations. And so, this is one example.  This can get very complicated in an algorithm,
and one of the things we've done with to help  developers is provide some tools where these
things can be all computed sort of automatically  and we can say whether or not we want it to, we,
we want this resizing of a vector to sort of  stick and, and stick around so that we can
compensate for different kinds of operations on  that vector, et cetera. And then by doing this we
can, we can really minimize like reallocating and  copy and copying data and things like that. So,
this is an important tool that developers have.  So, that was Matvec. For matrix-matrix multiply,
we have to con we have to build a matrix after  you do the product that is also represented,
it's also a stencil matrix, so it needs to have a  stencil representation. So, there's some stencil
algebra that has to be done up front, and the  way this works is kind of explained here quickly,
if I'm multiplying two matrices A times B, what  I mean by stencil here is you take a row of
A times B and you and represent it as a vector,  and that vector is the equivalent to taking the
transpose of B times a row of A represented as  a, as a vector, and this little identity here
is how we write a little section of code that  does a bunch of stencil algebra, and out pops,
if you multiply three matrices together, you'll  get a representation for what its non-zero stencil
is where each one of these stencil coefficients  is defined as a sum of products of coefficients
from the stencils A, B, and C. And all the details  about what the subscripts and superscripts are all
stored in this, this little code, and then  we use that to then, do the real multiply
app of on real matrices later. So, this is kind of  a preliminary step, and, and during this process
we can figure out which of these coefficients can  be constant, which ones cannot, don't have to be,
et cetera. Some other things we do in the code,  we, we only assume that we have two data spaces,
so think a fine space and a coarse space for  doing interpolation restriction or, or RAP or
these kinds of operations. Pretty much all of the  operations we need in hypre only really need two.
This allows us internally to limit our internal  box loop structure to only have three little
data spaces in it, which is nice. We again compute  necessary ghost zones automatically, we do some
aggregation of communication, and then in order  to mix the constant and the variable coefficient
types of matrices together, we have a little  tricky masking thing we do that I'll explain
now. So, a kernel looks like a sum of a bunch of  these triples for three matrixes, three matrices
multiplied by each other, and what we do is we  take each one of these little triples and we write
it as a coefficient, a constant coefficient alpha  times three variable coefficients, and this alpha
is, is what has the, the constant coefficients in  them what if we have constant coefficients in A,
B, or C. So, in particular, if all three  coefficients A, B, and C are variable,
this is just a 1, but if A, B, or C is constant,  we multiply them together and we put the product
in alpha, okay? And then the other thing we do is  then in the in the case of constant coefficients,
say, say the first one A is a constant coefficient  number. What we do is in this V1 place, we put
this a mask. So, it's, it's a vector that's either  a 0 or 1, and this helps us to know whether we're
on or off the grid, which is really important to  get, for getting the right answer. So, everything
in the kernel looks like something like, like  products and sums of these kinds of things here,
and we have lots of different cases we have to  take care of, you know. Some of this data might
live on a fine space, some on a coarse space,  so we get different combinations of these things
you know might have fine-fine-fine or  fine-coarse-coarse or fine-fine-coarse
or whatever, and we, we need to be able to handle  all those cases and that's all in the code. We can
also take advantage of the fact that you might  have structured matrices and will only do half
the computations as necessary. Okay, and then in  the kernels themselves, we have sort of two ways
of optimizing. One works well in CPUs, the other  works well in GPUs. In the CPU case, we do sort of
standard loop unrolling where you compute a single  coefficient by adding as many co as many of these
triples together as possible in, in one line of  code. What works better on GPUs is if we compute a
bunch of coefficients and there and contributions  to them all at once. This allows us to reduce the
number of current launches, and so this seems to  be a better way to go about on the GPUs. Okay,
performance, this is kind of some quick results  on a CPU for PFMG, and it's comparing to the main
branch. So, it was really important obviously we  were doing all this generalization and writing
these tools, but we want our algorithms in the  end that use the tools to be as efficient as
they were to begin with. And we've done that,  and it took a lot of sort of tricky stuff in,
in the inner kernels, but it, it works and  this is just showing that over a, you know,
a three- or four-month period we were working on  these optimizations and whereas in the original
code we didn't care about the optimization, we  were just trying to get correctness and we made
some pretty significant improvements. The plots on  the right are showing some results on the bottom,
so this is for a single node. So, it's 56 cores,  and we're just increasing the, the size of the
problem and this is showing the slowdown  relative to master of the different phases
of the algorithms, so the solid one is total time.  You can see that's less than 1 so the slowdown is
actually a speedup. The only thing that really  slows down in the new code is the setup phase,
and we'd like to do some more work to improve  this. But the reason this doesn't really make
much difference in the end is because the setup  phase is such for PFMG is such a small component
of the overall time, time that's involved here as  seen at the top, which is just plotting pure time.
We also did something similar for GPUs and got in  similar, similar improvements in the new hypre-3.0
version versus the, the master case. Same or, or  better slightly. And neither, in neither case it's
dramatic improvements. Okay, and I think this  might be the, well it's yeah this is the final
part of this semi-structured, and it's about the  new solver SSAMG. So, this is a solver that is
composed out of the PFMG and BoomerAMG solvers  in hypre. So, here's a picture on the right of
a bunch of different structured parts glued  together across these boundaries in some,
you know, potentially arbitrary way, and  basically, the way the algorithm works is within
a part we do semi-coarsening as we do with PFMG.  So, you see the semi-coarsening is not necessarily
in the same direction in each of the parts. And  then within the part we do two-point interpolation
like we normally do, and currently in the code,  we don't do any interpolation across the, the
part boundaries. So, our interpolation operator is  not a sum of two things, it's just interpolation
within a part. That's what's in the code right  now, and what I'll tell you about with the results
in the next few slides, we would like to have  this generalized so that there's an unstructured
component that allows us to interpret across  boundaries that will improve convergence. We've
seen indications that it can dramatically improve  convergence, so here for one case is reducing 20
iterations to 7, which is pretty significant. But  what we have in the code right now needs a lot of
work from an optimization standpoint, so this is  still work in progress. And this kind of shows
what happens when you have the full-blown case,  and this is what prevented us from implementing
this a long time ago. You can see you've got  lots of cross products here that are involving
structured and unstructured matrices, and it  just seemed but seemed like a big mess to, to do
all this, especially for a very specific solver  instead of what we have now, which has the more
general matrix-matrix support that we need. So,  anyway, this is SSAMG. And oh, one final comment.
The way we do this is we coarsen as I showed here,  construct a coarse grid operator, but then at some
point in the algorithm this is something that is  a set is a parameter that can be set. We switch to
doing BoomerAMG entirely. So, you come down the  V cycle in this semi-structured way and at some
point you switch to fully unstructured. Okay, so  through results, three results, they all are live
on a cube shown here with four parts. They have  a seven-point stencil that's anisotropic in X, Y,
or Z and combinations thereof. This shows how the  minimal processor decomposition is and, and here's
a, a decomposition across 32 processors, and these  results actually exist in a paper from 2023. But
what I'm gonna show you is an update to that, and  the performance is a little bit better, but it's
qualitatively the, the conclusions are the same.  So, the first is where we have anisotropy in X
direction all four parts here shown here on the  right, and really to, so here we have set up,
solve, and then this is convergence. So,  we have the left two plot time relative to
number of MPI tasks in the right is the number of  iterations. And really look at the, the solid red
and the solid purple. That's the best performing  SSAMG setup versus BoomerAMG. And the main thing
to see here is that in the setup phase we get a  significant improvement in time, and so overall,
we get an improvement in time as well. And  convergence solve phase is similar to AMG, it's
not, it's not faster. We'd like it to be faster,  but that's gonna take a little bit more work. Same
kind of situation now we have anisotropy and X  on the left and anisotropy and Y on the right,
and the conclusions are kind of the same again,  you get about a 7x speedup and setup, solve phase
are similar times between the two methods. And  then the last I have X bottom left corner, Y top

Okay, so, that's the semi-structured part, and now  I'm gonna switch to the last part, which is about,
about the mixed precision things we've added.  This is the other big component that we have
now in hypre-3.0. It's something we've also worked  on, I don't know, maybe four years or something,
I'm not exactly sure, we started working on this  a while back and obviously the reasons are the
reasons that a lot of other people are doing mixed  precision in their codes. The hardware is giving,
it has good support for low precision computing,  so we'd like to take advantage of that. The other
thing is limiting bandwidth so that we can put  more things on the GPU, you know, the, the more
computations you could put on a GPU, the better  off you are typically. Okay, so we had several
goals and, and several features that we added, and  this is kind of a summary of that. To start off,
let me say what the terminology, my terminology  is. When I say multiprecision, that's basically a
solver function or feature that uses one precision  at a time. So, hypre, even before hypre-3.0
was actually a multiprecision library where  that precision was determine determined at
compile time. Mixed precision on the other  hand is a solver function or feature that
has different precisions used at the same time  simultaneously. So, that's how I'll separate that
terminology. And what we did in this release of  hypre-3.0 is two, the two main things we wanted
to achieve. First was to do the multiprecisions,  the multiprecision part at runtime. And second was
also to have actual mixed precision solvers that  we provide so that we can get some improvement
that get faster and more memory-efficient solvers  in the code. Okay, so some features, you can
configure hypre with the mixed precision turned on  and it doesn't, you don't have to change any code,
it should run as before without any modifications.  All of the other thing we wanted to do is make all
of the compile time precisions we had before  available at runtime now so you can actually
switch between them at runtime, and that's what  this next line is about something we're doing in
the future and it isn't in there yet is, is assign  precision to objects like matrices and then have
things like Matvec automatically determine what  precision is ideal for doing the Matvec given the
precision of the matrices and the vectors that are  passed in, for example. And then we've added some
mixed precision solvers in hypre-3.0 and we have  more to come and I'll say more about that too.
Okay, the first part is about providing runtime  precision. So, I, again, I mentioned before,
you could do this in hypre at compile time before  by just come, you know, configuring it to be say
single precision, and that all worked already.  Now you to, to use a mixed precision, you just
have to use one of these two configuration  options in either the Autotools or the CMake
situation. As I said, this doesn't change in user  code. And then the next slide will give you more
idea about what's available now when you actually  configure things with mixed precision and what
you can do. So, when you configure with mixed  precision, you have several things that are
available to you that weren't before. So, I'll use  this term foo to represent any function in hypre,
so for example HYPRE_PCGSolve, all of it's gonna  be represented as foo here, and one of the things
you get when you turn on mixed precision or  configure in those mixed precisions you get
each of the fixed precisions available to you and  with these symbol names. So, Foo_flt, Foo_dbl,
et cetera, and so as a user, you can call  these directly and if you called Foo_flt,
you would do a you would get a single precision  version of whatever foo was. The prototype for
this function here is the same as before  except that the things like HYPRE_Real,
all the real types basically map to whatever the  underlying C type needs to be. So, in the case
of Foo_flt it's float. We also still provide the  symbol foo as it was originally in, in the code,

segments.text: It's really an honor to welcome Bill Henshaw to  our Finite Element Seminar at Livermore. Bill
is a distinguished professor at RPI. He got his  bachelor’s at Waterloo, then did PhD at Cal Tech,
then worked in a lot of really impressive places  that I've been: [IBM] Watson [Research] Centre,
Los Alamos, and I know him from, from when he  was at Livermore. He's done work on solving PDEs,
particularly on overlapping grids. He's the  primary, primary developer of the, of the Overture
Framework. And today he's going to tell us about  WaveHoltz, which is this interesting approach to
solving Helmholtz by filtering in time the wave  equation. So, it's a real pleasure to have you,
Bill. The floor is yours. Thank you, Tzanio. Yeah,  so I'm gonna tell you about, so I’ve been learning
about Helmholtz problems for the last two years,  so I’m going to tell you about this new algorithm
and some of the things that I’ve learned about  solving Helmholtz problems, which can get really
hard. So, first of all, does that work? So,  here are some of my collaborators. I work with
Jeff Banks, Jeff was actually at Livermore for a  number of years when I was there, Don Schwendeman,
and we have a student Ngan, who's a grad student,  and we work closely with Daniel Appelö who was
one of the originators of the WaveHoltz  algorithm. So, what's the motivation? So,
as probably many of you know Helmholtz problems  arise in many areas for wave propagation problems
looking for time-periodic solutions, so mechanics,  acoustics, electromagnetics. In our interest,
one interest for us is time domain Maxwell’s  equations, so we have developed some high-order
solvers for dispersive Maxwell’s equations on  overset grids, and well I should say here if
you if you have questions, please go ahead and ask  questions anytime. Unmute and ask a question. So,
the question is, you have a time domain solver,  the question is, well if you’ve worked hard to
get a nice time domain solver, can you turn  it in to find Helmholtz solutions, that is,
time-periodic solutions? So, how can you use  this time domain solver that you've written to
do that? And a lot of the publications, as Tzanio  mentioned I've developed this Overture Framework,
and a lot of publications are can be found under  publications and OvertureFramework.org if you're
interested. So, here's the basic question that,  I’m gonna step back and just do the wave equation.
Eventually we want to do the Maxwell’s, we’re  going to do the wave equation. So, here's the
basic question. Suppose I solve the wave equation  on this domain here and I have a periodic forcing.
So, the question is, have I just, do this periodic  forcing and integrate for a long time, will it go
the periodic solution? Well, in this case I have  Dirichlet boundary conditions around, so it's an
energy conserving problem. So, the answer is no,  it will not go to the time-periodic solution.
So, we need to do something else to make it go to  the time-periodic solution because on the right
here, this is the actual time-periodic solution,  and one thing you learned in high frequency,
if you look at the time-periodic solution,  you cannot really tell where the source is,
right? You remember from the video, the source was  sort of in between those triangles, but from the
Helmholtz solutions it’s really hard to tell.  So, just to give the answer away, so here's,
we can use this WaveHoltz algorithm. It uses  the time domain solver and then does a certain
time filter. And by doing that, we can converge  to the Helmholtz solution. And in this graph,
we'll talk more about what's actually showing  here, but where I say iteration on the bottom,
the iteration corresponds to each iteration  corresponding to solve the wave equation over some
number of periods and then filtering. Okay, so  each iteration is to solve the wave equation over
one or more periods and filtering. And I'm showing  results here for, for the fixed-point iteration
and GMRES and some theory. So, how do we do this?  Whoops, need to click here. So, our goal is to
find time-periodic solutions to PDE problems,  and there's enormous amount of work that's been
done on solving Helmholtz problems including  boundary integral methods, fast direct solvers,
domain decomposition methods. The basic takeaway  though is for really large problems we have to
use iterative methods. Those are really hard.  And there's this nice paper at the bottom by
Gander saying why, if you're not used, if you're  just used to solving Laplace equation with GMRES,
it's always gonna work, right? And you, you do a  Helmholtz problem well GMRES is not, not working

hard at high frequencies. There's something called  pollution errors I'll talk about, dispersion

make use of high-order methods. And so there,  there are, there are sort of specialized Helmholtz

limited in their, in their scope. So, here's the  algorithm, so the goal is to solve this Helmholtz
problem here. L is C squared Laplacian and omega  is a given real number given as the frequency and
we have some forcing on the equation, potentially  on the boundary conditions. So, what we do is,
we solve the associated wave equation where now we  have multiplied the forces by cos omega T, okay,
so in these wave equations we have cos omega T  and we're gonna iterate, in this case we're doing

in this case the algorithm is a little simpler,  we can just iterate on the initial condition,
so the initial condition I denote V of K where  K is the iteration number. We're gonna solve

the Helmholtz solution, okay. So, we solve  the wave equation, get the solution over time,

in green, they go up the vertical axis. So, it's  transformed all the original eigenvalues which go

Right, but that's, that's sort of the key thing  here is that we've done this transformation,
so it's an easier problem to solve by standard  methods. So, that's sort of the key thing. And so,
the basic fixed-point iteration, which we'll talk  about improving it, is the, the basic result is
that the fixed-point iteration will converge as  long as we're not forcing the Helmholtz problem

are the ones where beta is large in magnitude.  So, there are various ways to enhance the basic

and the algorithm still works, right? So,  that's sort of very unusual for wave equations,

segments.text: [Music]
[Music] Welcome everyone to today's seminar,  uh, so our speaker is John Evans. He's associate
professor at University of Colorado Boulder. Uh  he's interested in computational fluid dynamics,
structural dynamics, computational acoustics,  electromagnetics. Uh he's done quite a lot of
work in immersed techniques and isogeometric  analysis, and I guess today's lecture,
today’s presentation is uh related um to his work  on immersed and isogeometric analysis, and um,
welcome and thank you for accepting our invitation  uh to present. So yes. The floor is yours.
Thank you so much, um thank you for the kind  invitation. It's wonderful um to virtually be
here um today um, and as Boyan mentioned today,  I'm going to talk about a topic that's um really
at the intersection of many of my research  interests um, in particular in immersed finite
element methods um and isogeometric methods. And  the topic of my talk is particularly inspired by
the difficulty associated with implementing these  methods, and in particular if we want to retrofit
an existing classical finite element code into an  immersed finite element code, this typically takes
a ton of effort. And I'll um inspire um why that  is um the case a little bit later. Um and this
um really uh drove us to introduce this new um  immersed paradigm that we call interpolation-based
immersed finite element and immersed isogeometric  analysis. Um so without further ado I should
really um call out those that did the uh majority  of the work. Um so when this project um started it
was an NSF um funded project uh a few years ago um  really was a collaboration between um two teams um
our team at the University of Colorado Boulder,  which involved myself um and Kurt Maute and our
co-advised student at the time Nils Wunsch um and  a team at the University of California San Diego
um led by Professor David Kamensky um at that  time in the majority of the work done at the
UCSD side um was um done by Jennifer Fromm but  uh PhD students um Ru Xiang and Han Zhao um
also contributed to that effort, and the idea is  that the CU Boulder team really developed the um
pre-processing tools and I'll talk about what that  means here in a little bit, um and the UCSD team
really um was in charge of retrofitting existing  finite element code in this particular case,
the popular FEniCS platform form into an immersed  code. Um so just want to highlight again um Nils
and Jennifer did the majority of the work, um and  David um a couple of years ago um decided that
um he was done with academia and wanted to make I  guess real money in industry and joined Coreform.
Um so David um left the project um and J.S. Chen  at that time um became the UCSD um PI and led us
to investigate um some of these ideas in the  context of meshless methods, which I'll finish
my talk here today um by discussing. Um and then  uh a couple of years ago as well, an undergraduate
student who um then continued on with his masters  here, Ryan Caputo um joined the team and in
particular he investigated the use of so-called  curved um foreground meshes. And I'll describe
what that means here in a minute um as part of  his undergraduate research and into his master's
thesis. Um next slide, I always have to do this  um giving a talk either in person or virtually.
Come visit us in Boulder. Uh so I'm at CU Boulder,  and in particular I'm in the Ann and H.J. Smead um
Department, Smead Aerospace Engineering Sciences.  Um we're on the front range um in Colorado and um
aerospace in particular moved into a new building  in 2019, and we all know what happened in
um late 2019 and early 2020. So we all moved  out of this building and moved back in a couple
of years later. So the building really feels  new even though it's six years old. Um so it's
been wonderful to work here and we love having  visitors. So if you have any reason to visit us
at CU Boulder, please do. Okay. So with um that  precursory material um behind us, um let me talk
about the motivation behind um interpolation-based  analysis. Um so to begin, as you all know
um and this is an image that uh my old PhD  adviser Tom Hughes would show all of the time,
um classical finite element analysis requires the  generation of a high-quality body-fitted finite
element mesh. Um in very complex um applications,  for instance, like analyzing a submarine,
um this can require a ton of time. Um there  was a [unintelligible] study performed
in the early 2000s by Sandia National Laboratories  that actually identified up to 80% um of the time
required in design through analysis cycle really  was dedicated to taking um a design um a model
into an analysis model. Um now this is um but by  some measures a rather um pessimistic view, um
but there's many reasons um as well why classical  finite element analysis um sometimes can be a bit
challenging, and I should note that um generating  a um a high-quality, emphasis on high-quality,
um body-fitted mesh um is particularly difficult,  um and this is the case for geometrically complex
multimaterial um multiphysics problems  such as um shown here, a heat exchanger.
Um this was actually a geometry um courtesy of  nTopology which has really been investigating
um topology optimization approaches as um of late  and looking at really interesting designs. You can
think of fiber composite structures where you have  fiber composite layout in a matrix, or biological
um structures such as a bone. Um now early on in  my life, um I started in the field of isogeometric
analysis, and the big promise of isogeometric  analysis is that it directly employs um the basis
employed um in CAD, computer-aided design for CAE,  computer-aided engineering, and thus bypasses the
need for the generation of a high-quality  body-fitted finite element mesh. However,
um there is a caveat here. Um isogeometric  analysis, at least in its original form, requires
an explicit parameterization of the geometric  domain, and uh thus it can actually be applied to
the most common um CAD geometries described um by  NURBS. These are trimmed CAD geometries where you
basically have a bunch of NURBS patches, and then  you basically apply some scissors to those patches
and try to tie those um objects together. Um and  it turns out that doing so is actually a really
nasty, nasty exercise due to the fact that um the  intersection of two bicubic surfaces is actually
um in algebraic curve of degree 324 in physical  space or 108 in the parametric space of either of
those two NURBS patches that are coming together.  So this is a really nasty unsolved problem in
geometry, and the problem is even worse um  in 3D. Um and this is due to the fact that
um in CAD, um especially described using b-reps or  boundary representations, uh we describe volumes
by their bounding surfaces not by parameterizing  the volumes instead. Um so my old student Luke
Gangval used to joke that solid works really  should be called surface works as a result. So you
need to actually do some volume parameterization  or meshing anyways um when working with a b-rep
if you actually need to conduct um a volumetric  finite element analysis or isogeometric analysis,
what have you, as is required for analyzing  fluid flow, um acoustics, electromagnetics,
um deformation of a solid um structure, etc.  And immersed finite element and isogeometric
analysis um is another approach that bypasses  the need for the generation of a high-quality um
body-fitted finite element mesh. And the idea here  is that you instead define basis functions and a
non-body-fitted um background mesh that basically  encloses um the geometry of interest. Um and what
this means is that we can define the um basis  functions that are used to represent solution
fields such as displacement um for structural  mechanics problems, velocity and pressure for
incompressible flow problem on this nice simple  background mesh. And then the idea is that you'll
perform um integration over the actual physical  domain and utilize techniques such as Nitsche's
method, penalty methods, Lagrange multiplier  methods for enforcement of boundary conditions.
Now immersed finite element analysis is also very  powerful because it can be applied to problems um
that are thought of as out of reach. Um now out of  reach here is probably a bit of an exaggeration,
um but it's very hard um to do um using classical  finite element analysis and isogeometric analysis,
such as problems exhibiting a change in domain  topology. So an example of this um as shown in the
video here is when you've got um a heart valve,  right, um that you're um trying to model um the
deformation of um due to um blood flow um moving  past the valve, and when the valve is closed and
here it doesn't fully close in this video here, um  but you can imagine if the valve is fully closed,
um the fluidic domain um actually is topologically  equivalent to two cubes, right, because you
basically have these two cubes separated by this  this membrane or this valve. But when the valve is
open, then it becomes topologically equivalent  to one cube because now you can actually walk
from one side of the valve to the other. And if  you try to um treat this problem with classical
finite element analysis and in a paradigm such  as um an arbitrary Lagrange Eulerian approach um
where you actually move um the fluidic mesh um as  the um the valve and potentially the blood vessels
around that um are moving, what you find is you  often collapse many of your elements down to zero
volume, and this can lead a blow up of code. And  another example where you have a change in domain
topology is um when you're trying to actually  model say blood cells moving through a capillary,
and in this case um the fluidic um domain  topology changes as blood cells enter and exit
um uh the domain. Um so this is an image taken  um from a work from Hugo Casquero um on the
divergence conforming immersed boundary method  um where he developed this immersed um technique
based on um combination of isogeometric analysis  so-called divergence conforming discretizations,
which um I investigated my own PhD work, so super  exciting to me, but was able to handle problems
such as this where you actually have blood cells  moving through a capillary. And what motivated us
um for um this particular project was level  set topology optimization, um and immersed
finite element analysis um is ideal for this  application as the geometric domain does not need
to be parameterized or re-meshed at every design  iteration with a caveat of you may need a mesh
for integration, right, um and we actually take  advantage of that fact um in interpolation-based
analysis. But the bright side there is if you're  integrating, sorry developing a um a body-fitted
mesh for integration, the quality constraints  um that you need to have a good basis no longer
apply, right, so you can actually develop  pretty poor quality meshes and still be okay.
Now the primary challenge um of immersed  um of immersed finite element analysis
is implementation and it's challenging and  time-consuming task even for domain experts,
and the primary challenge um is numerical  integration over cut cells. So in this image here,
um we can imagine that the physical domain here  is depicted in gray, right, and we denote this
as omega. The boundary of the domain is denoted as  gamma. And we're using a background mesh here, um
which is um the boundaries of the mesh are denoted  in this light gray lines as seen here. And if we
have um background cells living fully inside the  domain, we can use say standard Gauss quadrature
rules um to perform integration. But for these  cells that are cut by the boundary of the domain,
um and what you see is like an example here where  the part inside the domain is denoted in gray and
the part outside of the domain is in yellow.  We can't use standard Gauss quadrature, and we
need to come up with um specialized quadrature  rules for every single one of these cut cells.
And as you might imagine, there's been many  different rules um that have been developed,
many different strategies, including for instance  um quadrature over body-fitted tessellation. Um
and you can imagine this tessellation could be  either um consisting of straight-sided um elements
or curved elements. And this tessellation is just  used for integration um in this purpose. You could
use quadrature over a quadrature or octree mesh um  which is um commonly employed in the finite cell
method, or another technique, for instance,  my research group has um investigated using
Green's theorem um to devise quadrature rules by  transforming volume integrals to surface integrals
and surface integrals to line integrals, and  line integrals to point evaluations. Um now with
all of these though, you need to actually have  specialized quadrature rules and not just that but
specialized quadrature rules for every single cut  cell, and um with many classical finite element
codes implementing these quadrature rules really  requires a reworking of the underlying code.
So um we asked ourselves, is there another  approach that we can take with immersed,
and this led to the development of the so-called  EXHUME project, um which stands for extraction
for high-order um finite element methods, and the  purpose of this project is to ease the burden of
implementing an immersed finite element code, and  in particular what it enables is one to transform
classical finite element codes into immersed  finite element codes with minimal implementation
effort, and the key technology underlying this  project is the concept of interpolation-based
immersed finite element analysis, and that's what  I want to talk about um next. That leads to part
two. So diving right in, um what we're going to  do now is um leverage um the Poisson equation as
a model PDE for exposition. So we're going to  consider this potato domain omega here, right,
and we're going to consider the problem,  the Dirichlet problem. Find the solution
U such that minus the Laplacian of U is equal to  F um where F is prescribed inside the domain and
U will be equal to a prescribed function G along  the boundary of the domain. And as all of us here
know, right, um finite elements methods start from  a weak form, and for this problem, um uh the weak
form is find U in the set of functions and H1,  right, so the set of squarable functions of square
integral first partial derivatives, such that  U is equal to G in the sense of trace along the
boundary of the domain. We can write this as find  U in the space of um functions H1 that are zero
along the boundary of the domain plus a lifting  of G inside the domain, um such that um for all
waiting or test functions V in H1 not um we must  satisfy integral over the domain of gradient of
U dot gradient of V is equal to integral of the  domain of F times V. So that's basically the first
couple of days of finite element analysis  101. Um and here we just um basically took
this PDE multiplied by a waiting function um and  integrated by parts. Um and the discrete problem
that we utilize for immersed analysis um much of  the time looks as follows um if we use so-called
Nitsche's method for weak enforcement of um  Dirichlet boundary conditions. So what we do
is we augment this with a so-called consistency  term that results from integration by parts, um
a symmetry or anti-symmetry term um that um acts  to make the stiffness matrix either um symmetric
um or the contribution is anti-symmetric plus a  penalty term um that restores coercivity um in
the case um of a symmetric Nitsche's method, and  we throw an H on everything, um in particular um
on our space um of uh discrete um trial solutions  um and test functions, which here are equivalent
um which is saying that we are going to represent  the solution field basically um in terms of a
finite sum of coefficients times basis functions.  And with quadrature-based immersed methods, which
are the most common, we define the Vh, right,  with respect to a background mesh. We can then
use standard element um Gauss quadrature on cells  contained inside the domain. And the challenge as
already articulated is integrating accurately  over the intersections of the domain with cut
cells. And one solution that I highlighted was  tessellating these mesh cell intersections with
quadrature elements, forming a foreground mesh,  and then over each of these sub-cells we can use
a standard Gauss um quadrature. So then if you  take a look at what this um looks like in terms
of implementation, what you see now we have to  do is we have to perform um integration over
each of those foreground cells, each of those  integration elements, and then we need to sum.
Now the implementation problem now is that the  quadrature here is defined on the foreground mesh,
but the basis functions are defined on the  background mesh, right, but standard finite
element data structures um and assembly  algorithms just work with one mesh, right,
um so we can't utilize these um standard finite  element um method data structures and assembly
algorithms, which led us um to instead turn  to these interpolation-based immersed methods.
And the primary want um behind the design of  these methods is basis functions um that are
used for assembly defined on the same mesh as the  quadrature rule. Uh the basis functions before
defined on the background and the quadrature is  defined on the foreground, and our approach really
um is quite simple. It's defined as follows. We  first just define a nodal basis on the foreground
mesh, and this foreground mesh can be of very poor  quality, but we can still define a Lagrange basis
on it. And then what we're going to do is we're  going to take our background basis functions,
and we're going to interpolate these background  basis functions into the foreground space,
or in other words, we're going to take each of our  background basis functions, which we'll denote as
Ni, and we'll interpolate them resulting in these  Ni hats, which you can think of as now as being
sum over the nodal basis on the foreground  mesh. And then we're going to just take our
background basis, right, and evaluate those  at the foreground nodes and then multiply by
the corresponding foreground basis functions.  So we're approximating the background basis
functions with these foreground basis functions.  And then we'll use the span of the interpolated
background basis as our solution space. And it  turns out that this ends up being equivalent to
a quadrature-based method if the foreground mesh  is fitted to the background mesh. So that means
that each foreground cell lies within a unique  background cell, and the foreground basis can
exactly represent all of the monomials um in the  background basis functions. However, we actually
get possible approximations and new numerical  methods. For instance, we can actually have a
reduced polynomial degree of the foreground basis,  we can say, hey, let's not worry about trying to
represent each of the background basis functions  exactly, um and this um allows us to use,
for instance, a reduced quadrature rule, um and  this can then in turn lead to a more efficient um
assembly. Moreover, what we can actually utilize  is a background unfitted foreground mesh, that is,
we can actually use foreground cells that actually  can straddle um multiple background cells. This is
not the case with um quadrature-based um immersed  methods because you actually lose accuracy,
um because you need to actually have an F accuracy  of your quadrature rule to maintain accuracy in
your final solution. So this gives us more  flexibility in mesh generation, and here I
should note this is generation of the foreground  mesh. So it doesn't need to be particularly
high-quality. So um to present a picture  to describe this a little bit more clearly,
um let's consider the case um of a domain where  we've got a square with a diamond cut out of it,
right, so the domain here is depicted  in red and then we're going to use
um a background um basis of quadratic or  biquadratic B-splines, and we'll define
um this background mesh here in black, I'm just  going to take one particular C1 quadratic um
B-spline. And now what we can do is, we can create  a foreground mesh, right, that is body-fitted
for instance by creating a triangulation such  that each of the triangles lies within a unique
background cell. So this gives us a so-called  background-fitted foreground mesh, and then we
can interpolate onto either a linear or quadratic  Lagrange space defined over this mesh, and we get

as FEEC, um not to be confused with like this  discrete exterior calculus which I guess is called

uh that Arnold and colleagues came up with  in like the early to mid-2000s. Uh so there's
uh several very important uh documents on this  topic. There's the Acta Numerica paper from 2006,

uh keep in mind that the Acta Numerica paper is  like 155 pages and the textbook is like 117 pages.

uh is effectively like constructed by uh computing  and alternating uh S linear map on the vectors in

Okay. So, in English, it's a transformation or  function which is a subset of the alternating

uh introduce some concrete ideas. So, first we'll  introduce the idea of a space of differential

[Music] So this is Freddie Witherden Freddie  Witherden studied physics with theoretical
physics at Imperial College London between  2008 and 2012 earning an MS MS degree with
first class honors in September 2012 Freddy  started a PhD in computational fluid dynamics
in the department of aeronautics at Imperial  College London under the supervision of Dr
Peter Vincent and graduated in December 2015  he’s currently an assistant professor of ocean
engineering at Texas A&M University Freddie’s  main research interests are in the development
of simple and efficient high order methods for  modern CPU-GPU platforms the primary vehicle
for this is the flux reconstruction approach  proposed by [unintelligible] at NASA in 2007
using the FR approach is possible to cover both  discontinuous Galerkin and spectral difference
schemes along with various new and novel methods  furthermore the approach is also extremely well
suited to the requirements of modern many-core  architectures so Freddy’s going to give a talk
on high performance asynchronous I/O for exascale  spectral element methods so how about okay thank
you Tarik for the introduction and today I’m  going to be talking about something a little
bit different traditionally I’ve been very much  on the solver side but today I’m going to be
talking about disk I/O so getting things primarily  solutions out to disk as quickly as possible and
discussing some of the tradeoffs that you have  to make there so I’ll begin with a quick bit of
motivation why do I care about writing large files  to disk well fundamentally my research interests
are around the simulation of unsteady turbulent  flows and you can see a few nice examples here so
you’ve got low pressure and high pressure turbines  rotorcraft aero-foils at high angles of attack
and insects all flows that have a large degree of  separation and these flows are really challenging
to simulate numerically and a consequence of this  is that these very large fluid flow simulations
typically require billions of degrees of freedom  so I’m showing here in the background an MTU T161
low pressure turbine cascade that we ran a few  years ago and this simulation required some 10
billion degrees of freedom to get good turbulent  statistics now what that means in practice is
that given this case had about 90 million  elements and was run with degree 4 solution
polynomials in this case they were hexahedral  elements what we end up with is 11.35 billion
degrees of freedom per equation we’re solving  the compressible Navier-Stokes equations so in
3D we have a total of five equations and thus each  checkpoint file comes out at around 423 gigabytes
this is big not too unpleasant but unfortunately  being in the world of turbulence what really
matters to us is not so much checkpoint files  but time averaged statistics as this is how we
do our comparisons with experimental data and this  fundamentally is what the engineers are interested
in in this particular low pressure turbine cascade  case we had to average for our partners at MTU 206
different quantities of which I’m showing a  few of these delightful things here on the
side and thus every time we want to write out a  time averaged statistics file you’re looking at
laying down about 17 terabytes to disk and  you need to make a call about how often you
want to write these things out more is certainly  better but when you’re writing out this much data
it begins to take a serious amount of time so you  have to begin to think about trade-offs how often
do I write these things out and that’s a trade-off  between how much time do I waste writing things to
disk versus how much could I lose if my simulation  dies 5 hours after I wrote my last time averaged
file so this is roughly where we are and why we  very often care about putting big files to disk
now I’ll just do a short interlude for a few  minutes on the tool that we use PyFR to do
these simulations and where this file format  development work has primarily been occurring
PyFR is a code that I started developing during my  PhD and is effectively a Python implementation of
the flux reconstruction or FR approach FR being  a discontinuous spectral element method that
typically is equated with nodal DG I don’t want  to go into too much detail about the code but I’ll
just note some of our features compressible  and incompressible Navier-Stokes arbitrary
order curved mixed unstructured grids typically  explicit time stepping can do implicit at a push
and in red I’ve just highlighted a few of our more  unique features that we have around things such
as stabilization shock capturing and also some  things on the physics side one point I would like
to make is that we do have in-situ visualization  capabilities that’s through the Ascent library and
this in many cases does enable us to reduce the  amount of I/O that we need to do but at the end
of the day we still need to write out checkpoint  files in case the simulation dies or the hardware
has a problem and we always have to write out  time-averaged statistics files and so there’s only
so much that in-situ visualization can get you in  terms of the structure of the code it’s a little
bit unusual because firstly it’s written in Python  and secondly we make very extensive use of runtime
code generation so all our kernels are in a domain  specific language and at runtime we translate
those kernels along with parameters about your  particular simulation configuration into C code
CUDA code HIP code OpenCL code and even if you  like Metal code that allows us to run on the full
suite of GPUs that are around today and then those  kernels are what are called by the Python outer
layer that is also responsible for disk I/O and  anything to do with MPI the implementation itself
is state-of-the-art in a few respects firstly  everything to do with kernels is internally
based around a task-graph structure this is to  reduce overhead and increase parallelism and
we play a lot of tricks with these task graphs to  enable things such as cache blocking additionally
beyond just doing runtime code generation we will  also do adaptive autotuning so we typically have
multiple implementations of a kernel and when we  go to run your particular simulation we’ll try all
of them see which combinations work best and do  all of that at runtime and this typically makes
us very robust to changes in hardware and hardware  architecture as the autotuning just absorbs a lot
of the differences between generations so  what this broadly speaking allows us to do
is heterogeneous computing from a homogeneous  codebase everything from a Raspberry Pi up to

segments.text: This is another edition of the finite element  seminar at Lawrence Livermore National Lab
uh today it's uh my pleasure to introduce uh  Denis Ridzal uh from Sandia National Lab um
I've known Denis for I don’t know 12, 13 years  maybe more now uh he got his degree from Rice
um and then he went and was the von Neumann  postdoc in Sandia a big honor and spent the
rest of his career there probably almost 20 years  at this point I don't know that's right yeah uh
he is an expert in optimization uh he has the  rapid optimization library the RO project software
that um he's leading and today he's going to tell  us about his work on R-adaptive methods but not
for improving quality for improving memory and  compression which is I think a very interesting
and relevant topic for us Denis thanks for  agreeing to present the floor is yours yeah
thank you Tzanio for the kind invitation uh and  uh first I would like to thank uh my collaborators
Graham Harper and Tim Wildey from Sandia Labs uh  this um project was sponsored by the Lab[oratory]
Directed Research and Development program at  Sandia it was a short two-year project uh but
I think we got some insights important insights  that I would like to share today uh all right so
um a little bit of history first uh and why did we  go down this route so uh about four years ago we
were working on a project where were trying to  design electromagnetic systems and um the goal
here uh and this was a DARPA project the goal  was to uh replace some of the optical systems
for night vision goggles with lightweight uh and  shorter length scale systems and the way they were
going about it was to replace some of the optical  elements such as lenses um with the so called meta
surfaces uh just a quick question can you see my  pointer it's important that I can point yes we can
okay so um here's a an optical stack um in let's  say night vision goggles and consists of a bunch
of lenses and we uh wanted to uh replace some of  those heavy and thick elements with very very thin
surfaces uh for obvious reasons you know weight  savings uh shorter length less torque on the neck
of the wearer and so um now what are these meta  surfaces well uh they are electromagnetic devices
with nanoscale structures and I have a picture  here on the left of one of them this is just a
very small scale model uh they're micron thin they  contain millions of so-called meta atoms and you
can see them here they have various um uh shapes  um and sizes and uh the you know unique feature
about this is that uh if you look at for example  one of these meta atoms is that they are all
extruded in one direction and so uh what uh some  of the folks on the project noted very quickly was
that um whenever they could mesh some of these  or whenever they could use uh finite difference
methods for the simulation of these meta surfaces  uh and that was possible for let's say uh square
shapes and such uh the performance was uh not only  much better in terms of speed but the memory use
uh of commercial tools finite difference tools was  uh at least an order of magnitude better than our
finite element simulators and so they could run  much much bigger simulations with those tools
versus our finite element methods and so that  motivated us to think hard about you know memory
use and uh also the types of meshes that are used  in this applications and so in this particular
application we have these extruded meshes and you  can imagine that uh there is a lot of repetition
in terms of the cell shapes um and we want it  to benefit from that on the memory side this is
important because not everyone has access to uh  very very large scale computers uh and even those
uh can run our memory quickly so uh here just a  few remarks on where we are with the memory use
uh you know modern computing has embraced massive  concurrency now we have million way concurrency in
many scientific applications Frontier and Aurora  are already running exascale calculations but many
um applications requiring the numerical solution  of PDEs uh are not limited by uh the speed by
the sheer speed of the system but actually by  the system memory and uh this is really due
to uh what I would describe as reductions in the  amount of system memory per uh thread uh over the
last 10 or so years and so um new approaches are  required to address this challenge and I should
just note that you know a lot of people are trying  to use neural networks uh to replace parts of PDE
simulations well uh that that won't really help  because in order to train the neural networks
you still have to run these massive simulations  with all the memory restrictions that they have
all right so um I think there's quite a  bit of hope here and I think one of the
fundamental uh shifts uh over the last 10 to  20 years is really helpful here and that is
that most HPC applications based on finite  element methods uh use uh modular libraries
now no one develops things from scratch  uh and so uh whether it is MFEM or deal.ii
or Intrepid at Sandia uh we all use libraries  and so the community here has um an opportunity
to address this memory challenge at its source  uh or a source which are the data structures
that are used for finite element computations uh  and to do so without significant changes to the
implementations of these applications so if you  can kind of do things underneath the hood uh to
reduce your memory footprint the applications  will automatically benefit uh there's a little
bit of a twist here which I may get to towards  the end of the talk and that is that also mesh
databases that we use to uh track um just the mesh  data have to sort of come along but I think that
they will join the effort if we're successful  in reducing the memory footprint on the finite
element computation side of things all right so  uh just very briefly some related work um we are
probably all aware of matrix free approaches  such as Jacobian free Newton Krylov methods uh
and MFEM's partial assembly uh they will seek to  avoid storage or Jacobians of PDE residuals and
then use matrix free uh or matrix free methods  uh for linear algebra so matrix vector products
instead of matrices of course that has to be  accompanied by the construction of uh matrix

going on in that area and there are just uh a  couple of um references on matrix free multigrid
preconditioners such as those by May, Brown,  etc. and Clevenger and Heister now there are
a few other related efforts uh one is well known  in finite element community and that is uh sum
factorizations the sum factorizations uh try to  reduce the cost in storing or computing finite
element based functions by exploring the structure  the lower level structure of those computations
um and there are several examples of uh uses  of those factorization such as in Bernstein
Bézier uh then isogeometric analysis and then more  recently in discontinuous Petrov Galerkin methods

somewhat tangentially related to this um our  data reduction techniques in PDE constraint

can uh do a little bit more here on the finite  element side uh so today I'll talk about two
uh contributions that are complementary to all  the related efforts that I described previously
uh and these uh two contributions are um go hand  in hand so the first one is we assume that we're
