segments.text: Morning, everyone. Welcome to another edition of the finite element seminar at Lawrence Livermore National Lab. This morning, it’s my pleasure to introduce Nat Trask from the University of Pennsylvania, who was at Sandia previously, and he’s part of various MMICCs centers. And he’s gonna tell us about data driven exterior calculus. And I guess this is an addition to the title “for probabilistic digital twins.” Nat, the floor is yours. Great. Thanks, Tzanio. And it’s great to be here. And I’m excited to talk to finite element enthusiasts. See, I’m Nat, I’m at U Penn, I just started here last fall, I still have a joint appointment as Sandia. I’m still involved in the DOE sphere. So a lot of the work that I’m going to present today comes from our MMICC center, it’s called SEA-CROGS. And one of the things that we’re interested in doing is building digital twins for systems of systems, which is kind of a catch-all for, for the kinds of things that pop up all over the place across DOE, where you have multiple subsystems that are coupled together. In particular, we think about E3SM a lot as a climate model, but yeah, so typically, these kinds of systems of systems, you’re thinking about each sub model coming from a huge legacy code, you want couplers that are non-invasive, and so on. So, if we’re going to build a digital twin of a system out of a system of systems, right, we want, you know, you talk to different people, you get a different definition of a digital twin, specifically, we’re thinking about something that a digital model that can make a prediction of a physical system, right. So, in some ways, that’s just classical finite elements. But we want this closed loop picture where you can make predictions close enough to real time, that you can also do real time data simulation on a certain time scale. So you have self-corrected models. So in order to do that, you know, everyone’s excited about machine learning, because it does stuff fast. But to do these specific, this specific class of models fast, you need the kind of guarantees that we’re that we take for granted in finite elements, right? So you need to prove that you get numerical stability, that you get physical realizability, that you’ll be able to extrapolate or at least know when a model is wrong, like know what the model doesn’t know. And in particular, you need to be able to handle multiskilled data, you need models that are probabilistic plumbing, to do UQ and so on. Right? So it makes sense that everyone’s excited about machine learning. But there’s, there’s a gap that needs to be filled in order to in high consequence kind of engineering settings to do it robustly. So, if we’re going to do that, we need guarantees, like the guarantees that I mentioned. And so it may be that deriving a physics-based model, you know, that intractable, it could either be that you know the governing equations are just way too expensive to solve, right, like climate physics, turbulence modeling, all of those like, you know the governing equations, but to actually resolve all of the relevant length scales is prohibitively expensive. Or it may be that you’re looking at a system where the physics are unknown. So for a lot of material science problems, we look at shock hydrodynamics, combustion, batteries, semiconductors, and so on, right. So this, this kind of archetypical problem shows up all over the place, our objective is to build in some exploitable structure, so we can prove something. So I talked about climate, there’s some other problems that we look at that have the same sort of system of systems flavor to it. You can look at mechanical assemblies, right, like a car or vehicle. You have fasteners, bolts, things like that, microelectronics co-design, when you look at very small scale circuits, you get two-way coupling, parasitic currents, thermal effects, and so on. Once you’re squashing a circuit down onto a very small footprint so that you can’t neglect the coupling across, you know, between different transistors and so on. And also, I’m involved in a SciDAC center applying these kind of ideas to fusion power, right. And in that case, you have a whole hierarchy of different models spanning different levels of fidelity, different length scales, and so on. Right, so all of these, right, you need, you know, just to motivate that, there’s a reason why we need a rigorous way to incorporate machine learning if we’re gonna couple all of these physics together. So, the primary tool that we’re going to use, we work with graphs, and graph neural networks are very popular right now. But graphs have the same kind of topological structure that a finite element mesh has. And so that that lets us play kind of finite element-style games. And specifically, the tool that we’re looking toward is Dirichlet and Neumann maps. So if you can, if you can learn a Dirichlet2Neumann map you can imagine, so the cartoon I have in the top left here, you have a bunch of subsystems, you’re going to punch out the weakest link, right? The most expensive bottleneck in the system that you’re trying to model. And if you can figure out the mapping between the state and the fluxes at the interface between this model and other models, then then you can couple things together, this is kind of classical and domain decomposition in hybridizable methods, mortar methods, and so on. So the idea is that we’re going…I’ll get into how exactly we do this…But this is kind of the blueprint that on a graph, we’re gonna hang a model on top of it. And you can, you can think about nodes of a graph as representing control volumes, and edges of the graph as representing fluxes in between control volumes. Um, so this is like dual to maybe a finite volume met a finite volume picture. And we’re going to enforce conservation structure, right? We don’t want, we don’t want to use machine learning to relearn conservation laws. We know conservation laws hold, empiricism really lives in the definition of fluxes. And so what we do is we, we’re going to represent fluxes in terms of a black box nonlinear flux, we don’t make any assumptions about the form of that race, or these nonparametric models in order to identify a nonlinear flux, but we stabilize it using a gradient flux, right. So think about this a little bit like, you know, by analogy to artificial diffusion, and the kind of tricks that we use all the time in finite elements to stabilize methods, right, so we’re gonna do the same thing now. And that’s going to let us prove things. Even though we don’t know what the actual governing equations are, beyond that they’re in conservation, conservation form. And there’s, this is gonna come in two flavors. So if somebody gives you a graph, you can think about circuit models, right? There’s a natural graph underneath the circuits, the network of the circuit itself. And there’s a whole class of models that you can hang, you can hang a model on top of that user-provided network. Right, so I, you know, obviously, electrical circuits, we did a lot of work in this front for like radiation hardened circuits, and things like that. But there’s also nonelectrical circuits, and so called circuit analogy models, so stuff like hydraulic networks, dash, spring dash plot systems, for mechanical systems, and so on. Right, but there’s a challenge that most data that you’re going to come across, most scientific data, there may not actually be a natural graph, right, you may just get a velocity field. Right, so somebody gives you PIV, or DIC, or, or something, right, they’ll give you a displacement field or a velocity field associated with a given problem. And so it’s not clear what we mean by a graph. So I’ll get into the math and exactly how we do this. But I want to just give this picture up front, to make it concrete, what the end result is going to be. So we use Whitney forms, which is a classical tool for mixed finite elements. And we use them to define control volumes. But the control volumes, you know, typically, you would do that by reference to an underlying mesh. Instead, we’re going to take the kind of logistic classification networks that people use in machine learning all the time like to say this part of the space is dogs, and this part of space is cats. We’re going to repurpose that to say to partition space up into a set of control volumes. In this picture on the right, you can see, the dashed lines are streamlines for flow paths the cylinder; in the background, you can see this sort of three by three set of control volumes, and as we train the model, we’re simultaneously solving for the partition of space and a set of unknown integral balance equations for what the fluxes are on those control volumes such that the sum of the fluxes is equal to zero. So we’re simultaneously learning the geometry and the physics without knowing what the governing equations are, we just tell it that mass is conserved in this case, that’s all you need to know for potential flow. Right? And it’s identifying in a totally unsupervised way that like, yes, the relevant control volume is this, the cylinder in the center, and then, and then it’s working out balance laws so that the learn model, which is the solid lines, agree with the dashed lines, with the data. There’s a lot of people who’ve contributed to this: Xiaozhe Hu, who, in particular, worked out the original data driven exterior calculus on graphs with me, that was kind of like our COVID project a couple of years ago, I probably won’t talk about the metriplectic bracket discovery. I’ll just say that the kind of geometric structure, you know, you can use this to learn geometric dynamics. So generalizations of Hamiltonians, Hamiltonian dynamics and Lagrangian dynamics and so on, including dissipative generalizations. The piece that I’ll get to at the end is the stuff we’ve been working on most in the last year or so which is, you know, once you have one of these models, how do you plumb it with a model for uncertainty and kind of come up with probabilistic extensions. structure preserving numerical integrators in  time and before explaining what we've done that's
new I thought I might just give a very brief  overview of the field so structure preservation
is a buzzword you attach to your proposals  and papers to improve their probability of
success but what does it really mean in this  context of initial value problems here are
four properties that an IVP might have that you  might care about so symplecticity reversibility
conservation and dissipation okay so what do  these mean well symplecticity is a property
of Hamiltonian equations arising in mechanics  and it's a bit complicated to explain sort of
at the lowest dimensional example that means  that areas of initial conditions are preserved
under the flow of the differential equation more  generally it means that the differential equation
preserves the symplectic two form but this is a  striking geometric property of equations arising
for example in Hamiltonian mechanics that  aren’t satisfied by general IVPs and this
is something that you might want to preserve in  discretization another property that you might
care about is reversibility so for example in  Newtonian mechanics if you negate the initial
velocity you just invert the direction of motion  or more generally if you think about this there's
somehow relationships between the trajectory  that a system takes and elements of symmetry
groups you might want to preserve this symmetry  in your discretization so these two I would say
symplecticity and reversibility have really been  uh the bulk of the focus of the field of geometric
numerical integration so in this field there's a  real Bible sort of the famous book that everybody
knows by Hairer Lubich and Wanner and maybe  90-95% of the book is focused on symplecticity
and reversibility but there are other structures  you might care about so for example conservation
laws that the equation preserves in variance  like energy or angular momentum and maybe a more
subtle one are dissipation inequalities that the  equation dissipates certain quantities for example
like entropy at a known definite rate entropy  can only increase and it increases with certain
rates given by the constants of the problem and  so what we're about in this talk Boris and I is
that we aim to devise structure preserving  discretizations for initial value problems
that preserve conservation laws and dissipation  inequalities on discretization in a symmetric
way without projections onto manifolds or Lagrange  multipliers which are some of the other techniques
that have been used in the past so to make this  concrete maybe let me just start first of all
with some examples before diving into how we do  it let's just see what we can do so let's start
with everybody's favorite ordinary differential  equation uh the two body problem described by
Kepler in 1609 or at least understood from data  in 1609 of course it was explained by Newton in

screen and with that Hamiltonian you induce the  associated differential equations now uh with the

structure preserving properties that we care about  so this system is symplectic it conserves angular

of these is quadratic and implicit midpoint  preserves quadratic invariance so if we start

framework is what's our approach for devising uh  discretizations that preserve these structures
so our approach is built on finite elements in  time FET and so just to clear up a potential
confusion right at the start we're not solving  for all time steps at once this isn't a global
space-time method we're still time stepping  exploiting the causal structure of the problem
it's just that at each time step we're considering  a space-time formulation and so to understand
finite elements in time let's first study  something maybe that is probably more familiar
collocation Runge-Kutta schemes for an ODE U dot  equals F of U okay so the big picture of many
many time stepping schemes is the following we're  at T equals TN at some point in our integration
we know U equals U N which might be a vector  of real numbers or it might be a function in
some balance space and what we want to do is we  want to compute the next value of the solution
U N plus one at T equals TN plus one so a big  picture a general idea that captures a great many
different time discretizations is the following  what I want to do is I want to find a polynomial
of degree S on the interval TN to TN plus one so  that takes in a real number and gives me something
in a balance space or a vector of real numbers  so I want to find a polynomial that satisfies
well first of all it should definitely satisfy the  initial condition that I know that U of TN is the
data that I have and then in order to determine  a degree S polynomial that's a vector space of
dimension S plus one so I need to specify S other  test conditions and exactly what test conditions
I specify will determine the discretization that I  get so once I specify S other test conditions then
that determines uniquely a polynomial and then  I evaluate that polynomial at the end point of
my interval and that's my next approximation okay  and so for a collocation Runge-Kutta scheme the S
test conditions that I might impose or I might  demand are that the ODE is satisfied pointwise
that U dot equals F of U at S chosen points in  the time interval between TN and TN plus one okay
so that's what a collocation Runge-Kutta scheme  looks like we can rewrite those conditions if we
wish in a variational way which doesn't seem  obviously useful yet but will be so we could
think about integrating this equation over the  time interval from TN to TN plus one and then
I want to enforce the condition at certain chosen  times in the interval so I'll do that with delta
functions and so here are my S conditions written  down with integrals and delta functions but now
if this holds for all of these S delta functions  it must also hold for things in their span so in
particular I could rewrite this in a more finite  element way of saying that I want the equation
to hold with this variational statement when  tested against the test functions associated
in the span of these delta functions okay so  that's what a collocation Runge-Kutta scheme does
a finite element in time scheme or sort of the  natural finite element in time scheme is I would
say perhaps simpler which is that instead of  choosing as your test set the span of a bunch
of delta functions if you want to impose S extra  conditions then you just choose polynomial of
degree S minus one and demand that the equation  holds for these test functions instead and this
is called the continuous Petrov-Galerkin  discretization in time this is kind of
the natural finite element discretization in  time why Petrov-Galerkin it's because I've got
distinct trial and test spaces the trial space is  continuous polynomial of degree S the test space

videos.title: FEM@LLNL | Numerical Solvers for Viscous Contact Problems in Glaciology

segments.text: So welcome to another edition of the finite element seminar at LLNL. It’s our pleasure today to have Dr. Gonzalo de Diego from the Courant Institute. Gonzalo is originally from Spain, did his PhD, not for Patrick and [unintelligible], and he’s visiting the Lab today. So if you want to meet with him, please let me and Cosmin know, he is a visitor of Cosmin, and he’s going to talk about numerical solvers for problems in glaciology. Interesting topic. So, Gonzalo, thanks for coming. And please take it away. Thank you very much, Tzanio. And thank you everybody for being here virtually and in person. Essentially. My topic today is viscous contact problems in glaciology. I’m aware that probably a lot of people haven’t worked with glacier modeling, so I’ll try to make that clear. But before I talk about glaciers, I just wanted to say that this topic is essentially the focus of my PhD thesis, which I finished in September at the University of Oxford under the supervision of Ian Hewitt and Patrick Farrell. Perhaps Patrick Farrell is a name that’s familiar to several of you. And I started a postdoc at the Courant Institute under the supervision of Georg Stadler. And the focus of my postdoc is no longer ice sheets, it’s sea ice. So ice seems to be my topic, but sea ice and ice sheets are very, very, very different physical processes. Anyways, today I’ll talk about ice sheets. So before I step into these contact problems that I want to talk about, I just want to motivate the mathematical modeling of ice sheets, why it’s important, and really we care about ice sheets because they are fundamental elements of the climate system, in particular, as I write here, the ice sheets of Antarctica and Greenland, all the massive ice that, if it were to melt, sea levels would rise by 65 meters. So as you can imagine, not just for the sea level rise, but for the energetic role that these massive amounts of ice have in the climate system. We’re very interested in understanding how they evolve. In particular, understanding how ice sheets evolve, not only implies understanding how they melt, but also how they flow. And as you see in this photograph to the right, which is a photograph of elephant foot glacier in northeast Greenland, you can see the ice sheet flowing towards the ocean, and it really looks like a kind of like bubble of honey, right? So this is a very good representation of ice sheet dynamics and the fact that ice actually flows when viewed over sufficiently long time scales. So this will be fundamental to understand the mathematical systems we’ll be working with. On top of that, we’re also interested in understanding how ice slides over the bedrock. This is a topic that will come up again soon, and also how meltwater, say, on the surface of the ice sheet, percolates into the base of the ice and also affects these dynamics. In particular, there’s a very interesting interplay between meltwater and sliding that is fundamental to understand ice sheets and their evolution. I’ll be focusing on a very particular set of problems that we’ve come to call viscous contact problems. So these are time-dependent viscous flow problems where you have a fluid in touch with a solid surface, and you allow for the possibility of detachment and reattachment. And below, I show the two main examples that are rising glaciology, which were the focus of my PhD thesis. And those are, on the one hand, marine ice sheets. Marine ice sheets are big masses of ice, ice sheets that slide from the continent into the ocean, and at a certain point they go afloat, as you see here. So a detachment occurs at a certain point due to the buoyancy of ice, which is lighter than water. This point is called the grounding line, and it’s difficult to stress just how important understanding grounding line dynamics is. You know, you go into like the Intergovernmental Panel of Climate Change, and you will see citations of actual technical papers on grounding line dynamics. There’s, people talk a lot about this possibility of a marine ice sheet instability that will create this charge of ice that starts accelerating in time under certain dynamic conditions. On the other hand, there’s a much more niche problem called subglacial cavitation, which I’ll talk about now. And in fact, even though I just insisted on how important marine ice sheets are for the purpose of mathematical modeling, I’ve come to enjoy talking about subglacial cavitation much more. It’s a very nice toy problem, and the masks become interesting. So for the purpose of illustrating what a viscous contact problem is, I’ll be talking about subglacial cavitation. And to make clear what subglacial cavitation is about, it’s essentially a process that occurs at the interface between the ice sheets and the bedrock. So if we zoom in to this interface between the ice and the bedrock, you can imagine that the bedrock is actually very bumpy, right. And along these bumps, the ice is flowing, and due to the effect of flowing and high water pressures of water from, usually meltwater from the surface of the ice that comes down to the base, these cavities form. And these cavities are important for two reasons. First of all, since the 1960s they’re seen as really one of the fundamental mechanisms in understanding the relationship between sliding velocities, what I call U b here, and sliding friction, what I call tau b. But on top of that, the fact that these are water-filled cavities, and the water pressure of these cavities are important for determining their geometry. We essentially establish a link between, on the one hand, the hydrology system under the glacier, what I said before, of this meltwater that percolates to the base, and the dynamics of the glacier, because as we will see later, this water pressure actually affects how the glacier slides over the bedrock. So this is a kind of toy problem I’ll be talking about. Now for the kind of mathematical and numerical modeling, but I’ll just quickly show another motivation of why we care about this. So as I just said, this is all about developing numerical schemes for this problem and the origin of this project back four years ago, four or five years ago, was the fact that these kind of viscous contact problems have only been solved with, until now, with a finite element, a module called Elmer. Elmer/Ice, maybe some of you are aware of it, and in particular, one of the papers where they solved this sort of glacial cavity problem, in fact, the only one that we, that we knew about, and you look at the numerical results, so I include a plot of this paper to the right. You have on the one hand, the geometry of the cavities. So that’s a top panel, and under it, you have these plots that represent the normal stress exerted by the ice against the bedrock. And if you look at these, you see that you have a lot of strange artificial numerical oscillations. So this seems to be inherent to the numerical results obtained with Elmer/Ice and as right here on the left, and that was really one of the main motivations for starting to look at this problem, the fact that existing results appear inaccurate and unstable. And on top of that, this problem has a very interesting mathematical structure, as you will see now, it essentially involves a variational inequality, and that opens up a lot of options for solving this problem in different ways. And in this existing literature, we realize that none of this mathematical structure was acknowledged. So this is essentially, I’m just trying to explain why we started working on this problem. And in a few slides, toward the end, I’ll show another figure that we obtain, and you’ll see that we obtain much cleaner results. So I’ll come back to this. But before I do that, I’ll present the mathematical model we’re looking at. So on the right, you see an idealized representation of the problem we want to solve, this subglacial cavity problem. What matters here is that the domain we will be solving, the PDE zone is omega, which is in white here to the right. That’s essentially the boundary layer of ice in between all of the ice sheets on top and the bedrock below. The geometry of the subglacial cavity, of the bottom boundary of omega, is given by h and in particular, what’s very important for us is to realize that it’s evolving in time, that we have a subset of the boundary of the lower boundary here marked in red, gamma a, which is where the ice is attached to the bed. Okay. Now in order to determine the evolution of this cavity, on the one hand, we have to know how the ice flows, and we use Stokes equations for that, since we considered a viscous flow, you see that there’s a nonlinearity here that has to do with the fact that glaciologists like to work with a power law rheology or the viscosity. So you get a kind of like p Stokes, or in this case, r Stokes, structure. But what matters for us here is the fact that we’re working with these contact boundary conditions that you see here. So it’s these three boundary conditions. What they tell us is the following. The first condition, which is the kinematic condition, essentially says that the ice cannot penetrate into the bedrock. The velocity has to go outwards. That’s why the normal component has to be negative, because it’s an outwards-pointing normal. The second condition, what it essentially tells us is that the ice can press against the bedrock, but cannot pull from the bedrock, right? That’s very reasonable. And finally, the third condition, this one here, says that either the ice detaches and u dot n is non zero, or the ice presses against the bedrock, but you cannot have both at the same time. This is a complementarity condition. So those are the contact boundary conditions. And then on top of that, what makes this problem special? Because perhaps many of you already recognize this kind of structure from elasticity. It arises in elasticity, a very similar problem. What makes this problem different is the fact that it’s a viscous problem, so we also need a free boundary equation to evolve the geometry in time. It’s not like elasticity, where once you solve the linear elasticity equations, you already get the deformed configuration. No, here we have to have a coupling between the free boundary equation and the Stokes equations. And the free boundary equation essentially tells us how the, sorry, how the cavity geometry determined by h, the cavity roof, evolves in time in terms of the normal velocity u dot n. So a very interesting fact that arises here is that when we discretize this problem, the way we treat u dot n in the free boundary equation and the way we treat u dot n in the contact boundary conditions are kind of coupled in a special way that I will make clear. But these are the equations we are solving basically. So just to make the numerics a bit clearer, we’re considering a very simple scheme where we decouple the Stokes equations in the free boundary equation. And essentially, we’re iterating in time. At each time step we solve the Stokes equation, we get a velocity field, we evolve the boundary, we deform the domain, and then we return to the Stokes equation. So the main takeaway here is that we’ll solve, we are solving the Stokes equations and the free boundary equations in this decoupled manner. So the basic questions that arise here is, and this is what the next slides are about, how do we solve the Stokes equations with contact boundary conditions? There’s many ways to do it, but what makes this problem unique is the fact that then we have to couple it with a free boundary equation. And this coupling is essentially something I’ll try to be as clear about as possible. Okay, so let’s talk about the Stokes equations with contact boundary conditions. Anyone who’s worked with these contact boundary conditions knows that the moment we formulate a weak formulation of the problem, which is what we want to work with since we’re going to solve this with finite elements, we don’t get a variational equality, but we essentially get a variational inequality. So if you look at this weak formulation, what’s important to notice here is that we seek the velocity in K, which is not a vector space. K is a convex subset of a vector space, where essentially we enforce what is, what corresponds with the kinematic contact condition and no penetration condition, okay? And, oh, next slide. Sorry. I feel like, whenever I touch this, I go to the next slide, but we have a variational inequality. But it’s more interesting to view this as a minimization problem, right? So this is essentially a minimization problem where we have two constraints. On the one hand, we want mass conservation, the divergence free constraint, which many of you probably work with, which are Stokes equations, and we also want the contact constraint, right? So these are two constraints. And the main point here is that, on the one hand, we have to choose when discretizing this with finite elements, a finite element space for the velocity and the pressure. That’s very well understood. But what will make this more interesting is the fact that the inequality constraint, so the kinematic contact condition, can be enforced in very different ways at the discrete level. So this is something we’ll play with now. But just before I go there, just to make things clear, I just want to say that I’m solving all of this in Firedrake, which is a finite element module in Python, pretty much an inheritor of f the kind of Phoenix philosophy, and for the velocity of pressure, I’m not going to make my life complicated, I’m just going to take Taylor-Hood. So that’s piecewise, continuous, quadratic polynomials for the velocity and continuous piecewise linear polynomials for the pressure. Much more interesting than this is the fact that in order to represent all the different possibilities for enforcing this inequality constraint, I’m going to introduce a discrete normal trace operator. So this is essentially a discrete representation of the normal component. Why am I making my life so complicated? Well, to make things clearer, this inequality constraint at the discrete level, once we’re working with a mesh, can be enforced in many different ways. The most natural ways is, as you see here to the left, I simply enforce this constraint on every point of the contact subset of the boundary. However, I can also weaken this, and I can say, well, instead of enforcing this inequality constraint at every point of the red boundary, gamma a, I could also simply enforce it at the midpoints of each edge, as you see here. I can also enforce it in a kind of average-wise way, right? So there’s many different ways in which we can enforce this. And again, why am I making my life so complicated. Can I ask a quick question? Please. When you say in both points, do you mean the degrees of freedom, all the degrees of freedom, or do you actually [unintelligible]? Well, it goes hand in hand, so the velocity lives in a space of piecewise quadratic polynomials. So to enforce it on every point, basically on every edge, I’d have to enforce it at three different points, right? [unintelligible]. Well, that’s a good point. It’s not always the case that you can get a quadratic polynomial [unintelligible] that’s positive and [unintelligible]. Yep. So you mean at all points. I mean at all points, yeah, yeah. So I’ll show later, like, so this is the next, that’s the next slide. So the most kind of obvious way to solve this would be to simply enforce in every point. And we can enforce this with a penalty method by adding the right penalty. And this would be like the most natural way to do it. But the crazy thing is that you have to evolve it with a free boundary, right? So that means that we have to solve it, say, hundreds or thousands of time steps. And when doing it in this kind of naive, straightforward way, it actually becomes very inaccurate, and this is a problem that I still haven’t come to understand very well, but I think it’s related to the fact that perhaps you have quadratic polynomials enforcing it on every point, perhaps creates some complication, because it’s unclear how that has resulted the level of degrees of freedom maybe. It’s something I don’t understand very well, but in this case, and one choice would be to enforce it on every point, but it’s a good point, yeah, you can also just reduce it to the degrees of freedom. I’ve also tried that, and it doesn’t work very well, though, so this is where the problem becomes interesting, that we can enforce this inequality constraint in many ways. And the kind of obvious ways to solve it don’t work that well always. So as I said before, here we had these three possibilities. So now I’m going to focus on this third possibility, on average-wise enforcement on edges. And if we do this, we essentially solve this minimization problem where our constraint becomes this kind of average-wise statement of the inequality constraint. And one very nice way to solve this, at least in Firedrake it becomes very easy to implement, is by enforcing a Lagrange multiplier. So if we look at the first order optimality conditions of this minimization problem in terms of a Lagrange multiplier that enforces this inequality constraint, we essentially get this system where you can see, on the one hand, that the Stokes equations are now a variational equality so the first two lines where we have an additional term that enforces the inequality constraint. So you have an additional kind of forcing term involving the Lagrange multiplier lambda h. The Lagrange multiplier lambda h, as you can see at the first line, lives in a piecewise constant space of polynomials along the boundary. This is a natural consequence of enforcing an edgewise average statement of the inequality constraint. And what’s very nice is that you essentially get an average-wise statement of the contact conditions, as you see down there. So this is essentially analogous to those three contact conditions that I showed at the beginning, but now it’s stated in this kind of edgewise average way where each e is an edge of the mesh right. And this you can easily rewrite in terms of this max operator as a nonlinear condition. So this is what we implement directly in Firedrake, simple to implement, and it kind of shows how you can go from contact conditions, which are these set of inequalities, to a nonlinear equation, right? So now we have an equation, and this is what we implement in Firedrake, okay. So until now, it’s all about the discrete Stokes equations. But as I said, one very important aspect of this problem is that we’re constantly coupling with a free boundary equation. So how does this coupling work? So the free value equation is essentially at the continuous level, what you see up here. And I’m just going to choose a very simple discretization, so finite differences forward Euler, so you get what you see below. And here, the interesting thing is that, again, we have to introduce a normal velocity component. And what turns out to be fundamental to get an accurate algorithm for these viscous contact problems is what I call, on the one hand, a notion of compatibility. So the choice I make for the representation of this normal trace operator actually has to be compatible with the choice I made before for the way I discretize the inequality constraint. So remember, it was average-wise. And on top of that, this free boundary equation in this in the context of this subglacial cavity problem is actually advection problem in the sense that we’re advecting the cavity roof in the direction of the flow. So we also have to take into account the fact that we need to stabilize this problem. So these are the two constraints that we have to take into account when constructing the discrete free boundary equation. And how do we do that? Well, it’s kind of obvious, right? On the one hand, we use the average-wise velocity on each edge. Why do we want to do that, because for this average-wise velocity, we’re satisfying the contact conditions exactly. So we have a clear distinction of regions that want to detach and regions that want to stay attached because we’re solving those contact conditions up to machine position with a Lagrange multiplier. So what makes it more interesting is the fact that if you look at the notation I take here on the right panel, the edge e i is immediately downstream of the node h i. So, oh, I sorry, I touched the screen and something happened. It’s, it’s, it’s, yeah, actually, anyway, so if you, if you, if you take a look at my notation, the discrete free boundary is solved for each node h i, and if you look to the right the edge, e i, from which I choose the velocity is located immediately upstream, because I’m assuming that the flow goes from left to right of the node. So this is essentially a form of upwinding. So this is kind of our solution to this issue of, on the one hand, enforcing the contact conditions at the level of the discrete free boundary by choosing this average-wise velocity, and on the other hand, stabilizing by choosing the velocity associated to the edge immediately upstream. So yeah, so this was our way of solving the problem of coupling the free boundary and the Stokes equations. And now I’ll convince you that it works well by showing you a video, which I have to change window actually, actually have it to go a few more. Oh, sorry. I feel like we already knew how to do this, and now it’s not working that well. Actually, actually, so, yeah, there was a little issue with the presentation, and the video wouldn’t come up, so I just opened it. So in this video, on the one hand, you have a cavity at the right panel. So now the cavity is attached, so you don’t distinguish the cavity from the bedrock and what you see below, unfortunately, that the legend is associated with the PowerPoint, so I don’t have it here. In black you have the normal velocity, so this is at time zero, I still haven’t played it, so this is where the ice wants to detach. And in red, you have the Lagrange multiplier that represents the force exerted by the ice against the bedrock. So here you can already see that at t equals zero, we have a perfect distinction of regions that want to detach and regions that want to stay attached. And as you see, as I play this over time, you see that this changes. So actually very crazy problem, because we have actually singularity at the reattachment point. It’s that peak that you see there with the Lagrange multiplier and, um, anyways, with the video, I won’t show it again. It’s a bit complicated. Or maybe now I just have to do this, right? [errant repeated word actually] Oh, it’s there. But it doesn’t matter [errant repeated word actually] Sorry about that. Don’t worry. This is just a classical issue of compatibility with PowerPoint and Windows/Mac. Anyway, that was just a video to show what these simulations look like. And actually, we return to that image that I showed before, where I compared with Elmer/Ice, you can see that the steady states we find here, what you have is sigma n n, which is essentially the force exerted by the ice against the bedrock. And it has to be negative. Actually, when you’re solving it in this neat way with the Lagrange multipliers, you’re exactly enforcing the contact conditions at every point. So it’s very nice to see that actually these numerical results essentially show that we don’t get those wiggles anymore, and also that minus sigma n n is strictly positive or, well, it’s non zero, nonnegative. Sorry. So actually, essentially, this means that the contact conditions are enforced exactly, and that turns out to be very important for a robust and accurate computation. Okay, so I’m going to return to this idea of the subglacial cavities being fundamental for glacier sliding by showing you an application of this algorithm where I’m going to compute what they, what people in glaciology call a friction law. So a friction law is this relationship s, between, on the one hand, the sliding velocity u b, u b is the velocity at which the glacier slides over the bedrock, and tau b, which is a friction exerted by the bedrock on the glacier, and oftentimes you have additional parameters involved in this friction law. So in particular, for subglacial cavitation, if you do a kind of nondimensional analysis of the problem, you realize that the other factor that’s important here is what people call the effective pressure. So what is the effective pressure? The effective pressure is a difference between an overburdened ice pressure, which represents the weight of the ice sheet on top of the cavity, and the water pressure, which is the pressure exerted by the water inside the cavity upwards, right? So it’s this difference, this effective pressure, that turns out to be a fundamental variable in subglacial cavitation, and we can find the form of f essentially by choosing different pairs of sliding velocities, which is an upper boundary condition, as you see here, and effective pressures, computing steady states of the cavities and then finding tau b by integrating the pressure exerted, the stress exerted by the ice sheet against the bedrock in the horizontal direction. If we integrate that, we find the friction. So if we do this for many steady states, we get something like this. So each dot here is a steady state. The left panel, the left axis, sorry, the vertical axis is a nondimensionalized form of the stress. It turns out to be a good way to nondimensionalize it in this way. The lower panel shows a sliding velocity to a particular power that has to do with the power law exponent of the viscosity, again divided by the advective pressure. And as I said, each of these points is a steady state for this subglacial cavity system, so we have a geometry. And it turns out that along the initial segment to the left, which clearly has kind of linear looking, but it’s a power law form. What we have is that the ice stays attached to the bedrock, and it’s only when you reach a critical velocity or effective pressure you start having detachment you get to um maximum, which actually represents the inflection point of the sinusoid bedrock, where you have the maximum friction, and then you start having what they call this weight, this rate-weakening regime where an increase in velocity or pressure, water pressure, involves a decrease in friction, and you see that the ice detaches more and more as you advance. So something you all probably notice is that we start getting again these kind of wiggles. This has to do with the fact that you need an incredible amount of refinement near the contact point because the singularity that you saw before in red of the stresses becomes more and more dramatic, so you have to refine like crazy, essentially, because a small change in the contact point enriches a large change in tau b in these regimes. But yeah, this is essentially the numerical results for this glacial cavitation problem. And now, for the last three, four minutes, I’ll just talk about the other topic. I only have two slides. But as I said before, marine ice sheets are a very important problem. This is an example of what friction profile of the marine ice sheet, of the Antarctic ice sheet, looks like. So essentially, if you were to cut here in Antarctica from point B to B prime so this is what they call the West Antarctic Ice Sheet, you would get this profile that you see here, where you have two big ice shelves which are floating ice sheets. So one is a Ronne Ice Shelf here, which corresponds to this area, and the other is a Ross Ice Shelf. If you look at this panel on the left, the color represents the ice velocity, and you can see that the ice flows incredibly fast in those regions. So these are regions of fast-flowing ice from the continent into the ice shelf, into the ocean. This is what causes sea level rise, essentially, right, because grounded ice does not contribute to sea level, but as soon as it starts floating, it does contribute to sea level. And as I said before, there’s a lot of interesting dynamic processes here. On the one hand, these ice shelves serve as buttressing that keep the ice on the continent. Yet sometimes they collapse. There’s something like a dramatic, sudden breakage of a large chunk of ice, and that changes a kind of force balance and creates more flow. So these are very important components of the climate system. And we’ve been studying these systems by solving what we call this parallel slab marine ice sheet, where we just consider an idealized situation where ice slides from this inclined slope, and it goes into the ocean. And what you see here is essentially what the steady states look like. At a certain point they detach, and then the ice starts thinning as it flows into the ocean. And something that we looked at with our solver were flux-thickness relationships. So that is, if I find a steady state, then at the grounding line, I have an ice thickness. I have an ice velocity. And this relationship between flux and thickness is very, very important, because it tells us a lot of information about how a change in the grounding line configuration changes the amount of flux into the ocean, which is essentially what matters for sea level rise. Also from a mathematical modeling point of view, where these flux-thickness relationships, you can actually solve a simplified free boundary problem. This kind of acts like what they call a Stefan condition in these free boundary problems. So a very interesting system. And as I said, I don’t want to show too much, but we’ve basically been studying what these grounding line flux functions look like for different regimes. Sometimes the ice is dominated by sliding, so there’s hardly any shearing. But other times, the ice is stuck on the bedrock, and you get more of a shear dominated flow, as you see here, and you can already see here that the geometries change dramatically. So it’s very interesting to see how these flux-thickness functions also change. And yeah, that’s basically one of our projects that should be out soon, but I won’t talk too much about that, and I’ll close the presentation. Now I realize that maybe I was a bit faster than I expected, but yeah. So the conclusions are that in order to compute these viscous contact problems accurately at the numerical level, what we did was enforce this discrete piecewise constant contact boundary condition and use that formulation of the contact conditions for solving the free boundary equation. So essentially, there’s this kind of coupling between how you solve the contact conditions and how you evolve the boundary. And one aspect of this problem which I didn’t really talk about, but essentially, we find steady states by solving the system in time. So we allow it to advance from an initial state into a steady state. And this is very time consuming, and at times it’s really not robust. So I think one of the future improvements will be to figure out a way of coupling this variational inequality and free boundary equation at the numerical level. That is, find a way of posing a nonlinear problem where our unknowns are the flow solutions, right, the velocity and the pressure, perhaps the Lagrange multiplier, but on top of that the free boundary. So I think this will require ideas perhaps from friction, shape optimization, right? We’ll have to evolve the geometry of the problem as well. It’ll be one of the additional unknowns, but this will allow us to do more stable time stepping schemes, perhaps by doing implicit Euler instead of forward Euler. But on top of that, for finding steady states, perhaps we can find steady states directly with Newton’s method, right, solving for the geometry and the flow solutions. Thank you, Gonzalo. Thank you very much for your attention. Okay, so questions, if you’re online feel free to unmute and just ask. Well, I guess you know the I think you’re, you’re the way I understand it, your issues with the contact where, if you try to enforce it, if you tried to enforce it basically on a noble basis, and you found that that was unstable, and that, I guess that’s that you would actually have an issue if you, if you try to enforce it kind of on your average basis, that could also produce an instability because you kind of don’t have the same number of constraints as you have degrees of freedom. So I guess, do you have an insight as to why you had an instability when you tried to enforce it modally. Yeah, so first of all, when you set up this mismatch between degrees of freedom, I think that’s okay, because what you have here essentially a stability condition, an n sub condition, and we can prove that that condition does hold between the quadratic polynomials for the velocity and the piecewise constant polynomials for the normal component. So I think in that sense it’s stable. The issue regarding the quadratic polynomials and the direct enforcement of the contact conditions. You know it has to do with the fact that, let me see what the best way to show this is. So here you can see that I have, in black, a normal velocity. This is at time t equals zero. videos.title: FEM@LLNL | Data-Driven DG FEM Via Reduced Order Modeling and Domain Decomposition

segments.text: Welcome, everyone to the FEM at LLNL seminar  series. We've, we've been doing this for a
couple of years now. And we haven't run out of  speakers yet, so we're gonna keep doing it. I'd
like to introduce Kevin Chung. He's a postdoc  researcher in the Materials Engineering Division
at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory.  Prior to joining Lawrence Livermore in 2023,
he was a postdoc at the University of Texas  at Austin. He received his PhD and MS in
theoretical and applied mechanics from University  of Illinois at Urbana Champaign in 2017 and 2015,
working with Professor Jonathan Freund.  In 2014, he received a BS in mechanical
and aerospace engineering from Seoul National  University. So please welcome Kevin Chung. And
he's going to talk to us about some DG work he  has been doing. Go ahead and take it away, Kevin.
All right, thank you for the introduction, and  hello, everyone, I'm really glad to have this
opportunity to present our work to all of  you here. Initially, the title was the best
robust scalable physics simulator. But um,  we kind of ended up changing this title to
this data driven DG-FEM as it might describe our  method better this way. And so throughout this,
this talk on you will see how this reduced order  model and the domain decomposition are combined
to produce this data driven finite element method.  So our work is a part of a big project of about 30
people from many divisions in the Lab, named as  a science of scale up. And the main overarching
motivation of this project comes from the fact  that there are like thousands of new technologies
being published every year, but only few can  actually get publicly deployed to the industry.
And even if they get deployed to the industry, it  takes about like 35 years to be commercialized.
So this is one example. Actually, this is the  main target technology that we care about in
this project. We have this new carbon capture  technology using a triple the periodic minimum
surface geometry, manufactured by 3d printing.  And we demonstrated and validated this efficiency
after the structure of posting experiment and  the simulation at the laboratory scale. But um,
if you just follow the conventional scaling  up process, you will take a decade to like
deploy this into the industry scale as large  as those existing carbon capture operation
facility like this. So in our project,  we would like to tackle this challenge,
see if we can bridge the gap to translate  these innovations to the real world impact.
And there can be many aspects in this challenge.  But one major bottle bottleneck is this pilot
staging, where we are deploying this new  technology from laboratory scale to the
industry scale, you can't really guarantee that  the performance will remain the same. And there
also can be some failure modes emerging from the  larger scale that we've never experienced from
the smaller scale. So what we typically do is to  build up this intermediate scale, where we call
a pilot plant, so that we can demonstrate and  assess the performance and any possible risk.
And the problem here is that building this pilot  plant itself can take years to design, construct,
or operate. And it may require multiple stages  of this pilot plant. And so we want to accelerate
this deployment by replacing the physical pilot  plant with a computer simulation. And so with
this E pilot, we can not only demonstrate the  performance, but also we can fit our analysis
back to the entire design process. We hope to  predict a scaling behavior, or like detect the
failure modes, and reflect this analysis back  to the design process. And all of this with a
much shorter time than the physical pilots. Now if  we just tried to use the conventional simulation
method, such as the finite element method, finite  [unintelligible], finite difference and whatnot,
it's actually too expensive for this E pilot. In  this laboratory demonstration, we use the finite
[unintelligible] method on the grid of a million  cells and it took three days on 144 processors and
just for simulating 30 physical seconds. So, if  we consider the industry scale now, which is seven
orders of magnitude larger, the computation of  course can be just intractable. And this is also
true for those intermediate pilot scales as well.  And we might attempt to rely on some approximation
on a smaller scale, such as our LES simulation  with closure modeling or homogenization approach,
but these approximations, they can become  often like render a simulation inaccurate,
where it is a larger scale system. Within machine  learning is a promising alternative, becoming very
popular these days, there are a lot of methods  coming up every day and which I think is worth
exploring, particularly like these physics  informed machine learning techniques, they are
quite promising in that they can identify the new  physics only from the data, and where we do not
have enough knowledge about that. And these are  two examples, where it is successfully identified
the Navier Stokes equation only out from the  snapshot data. And in the case of this near
operator, it is actually quite amazing that it can  predict even higher resolution solutions, the much
higher resolution, than the training data or by  interpolating like the smaller scales. Although
when it comes to this scaling up problem, we’re  kind of faced with this particular challenge,
that we actually do not have the data available  for the pilot or the industry scale. So without
any larger scale data that we can feed into  the neural network for the training, we need to
somehow extrapolate and scale only from the small  and large scale data. So how do we do this, so we
focus on the fact that we kind of already know the  physics or the equation quite well, like this is
already well demonstrated in both experiment and  the simulation at the laboratory scale, we just
need to solve it efficiently and combine the small  scale prediction into a larger system. And so this
is where the main components of our method come  into play. First, we use the reduced order model
or ROM, to solve a the equation efficiently based  on the data, and then now we combine them into a
larger system using the discontinuous Galerkin  domain decomposition. And, as I mentioned in the
title, this will turn out to become a data driven  DG finite element method. And so I’d like to first
introduce the ROM and then I'll talk about how  we employ the domain decomposition for the ROM.
So to introduce the ROM, I’d like to start  from the conventional finite element method
as a reference to compare. And we have  the Poisson equation as a toy example,
which I will use all throughout this talk. The  standard Galerkin projection is to project this
equation onto the test function where the  post solution and the test functions are
defined in the same finite dimensional function  space. And in order to make this function space
close enough to the original infinity  [unintelligible] that function space,
we basically split the domain into many  mesh elements, like typically over a
million for 3d simulation, with this  simple geometric like triangle square,
or some polyhedrons in the 3d cases. And we'll  sign here analytical polynomial bases to the
each mesh element and the resulting discretized  system becomes very huge, which takes a long time
to solve. So now on the reduced order model comes  into play at this point where we replace this
polynomial basis with a data driven basis that can  represent a solution in much more efficient way.
So how do you make this basis out of the data.  To construct the basis out of the data, we use
this method called proper orthogonal decomposition  or POD. And this method has been out there for a
while, probably some of you already know, like,  this as a principal component analysis. And,
in essence, we basically apply the singular  value decomposition to this snapshot matrix,
where each column is a sample solution from a  high fidelity simulation. And if we apply the
POD to the snapshot matrix, then we obtain this  orthonormal matrix by which identifies the major
axis of the snapshot scattering. In this example  of the 2d vector snapshots, we can obtain the two
major axes associated with the scattering and  the scattering along the second direction is
quite small. So, we might neglect this direction  and then approximate all the snapshots with only
one direction, which still gives us a quite good  representation of all the snapshots. And this
information of the scattering is actually stored  in this singular value matrix or singular value
spectrum. And in this another example, for the  flow past a cylinder, when we performed the POD,
we actually see that singular value spectrum  is decaying really fast. And in indicates that,
like over 99% of the snapshot magnitude can  be represented by using only one or only a POD
pieces. So in essence, the POD can reveal such a  low dimensional manifold on the length of physics,
and we can use them as a data driven basis that  effectively represents a solution. So now, we can
build a reduced order model with this POD basis.  This is essentially the same as the conventional
FEM formulation. And the only difference is that  we replace the original polynomial basis with a
new POD basis. Here we have the standard FEM  formulation as a full order model and I have
this weak form matrix vector system. And this is  supposedly very large, as shown up here. And so
it takes time to solve this system. And now,  we approximate the FOM solution and also the
test function, which is a linear combination  of the POD basis and take its coefficient as
the wrong solution and the wrong test variable.  And this way, we can project all the large FOM
operator into this POD basis space, leading to  this much smaller and dense operator. So, now,
this is an example for the POD, the Poisson  equation. And just for the demonstration,
we generate the samples by varying only  one parameter within this right hand side,
and we obtained a POD basis from the snapshots and  project the FOM operator onto the 10 POD basis,
which was originally 5000 dimensions. So using  this ROM, you can basically make a prediction
100 times faster with a decent accuracy, or even  for a perimeter value that is like outside of the
training range. So now this shows the premise of  the ROM in accelerating the simulation. But by
itself, ROM cannot predict for a larger system  than it is trained for, so we still need to
answer this question: How do we use this ROM to  make the prediction for the larger system. So,
this is where we bring the concept of the domain  decomposition. We have this our large domain,
which is so big that we cannot obtain a  snapshot data out of the high fidelity
simulation or experiment, we split this into  a smaller domain or smaller subdomain like a
repeatable unit component. And then that becomes  small enough to generate the snapshot data for the
ROM training. Then just like the last slide, we  can create a ROM for each subdomain, solving the
physics equation at each subdomain. And now that  we decompose the domain, we kind of had to take
care of this interface between the subdomains  ensuring the continuity or the smoothness over
the interface with the corresponding reduced  order model. So compared to the other data
driven method, ROM formulation is actually  very similar to that of the FEM formulation.
Using the same Galerkin projection and only  difference is the choice of the basis. So,
in some sense ROM has a really great potential  to be a finite element as long as the interface
is appropriately handled. So, this is one of  the main agenda in the next couple of slides.
And so, um, there have been some active research  for this combination of the ROM and the domain
decomposition and I’d like to introduce some of  them very briefly. And the first one uses this so
called steady condensation domain decomposition.  And here is the main essence of how they treat the
interface between subdomains. We had the linear  physics equation or generic bilinear form on the
right hand side, and we split this solution  into the each subdomain M and each subdomain,
we further the split solution into the particular  end of modular solutions, the particular solution
only take care of the right hand side having the  homogenous boundary condition, and on the other
hand of modular solution will only take care  of the boundary condition with a zero right
hand side. So, in essence, we basically have a two  separate ROM basis for the interior part and the
interface of the subdomain. This is the example  application to the linear elasticity problem,
which was quite successful [unintelligible] a  ROM for this are two unique components, which
you can construct is a lattice patch structure.  And you can even optimize its design with over,
like, 100 times faster computation time. And here  although there is a limitation which is separating
the solution like this is actually only possible  for the linear system and the extension to the
linear system is kind of not straightforward. And  this is another type of the domain decomposition
where we take the linear, least square Petrov  Galerkin projection. Here, we start from the
discretized physics equation and the interface is  defined to be some overlapping degrees of freedom
between the two subdomains like this, and we stick  with, we basically seek a least square solution
for each subdomain under the equality constraint  for the interface, and we basically apply some
optimization method for this equality constraint  minimization problem. And the strength of this
our domain decomposition is that it doesn't care  about the discretization method, we can bring any
grid based method like FEM, finite difference  M or not. And this is also applicable to any
general nonlinear physics. Here it shows all  the successful demonstration of the LSPG method
on Burger’s equation. And here they even used a  neural network based nonlinear [unintelligible]
basis, achieving a much better accuracy than  the standard POD basis. So, here however,
this method in general kind of has some difficulty  in enforcing the continuity. The experience that
if the continuity is strictly enforced, the  solution often leads to become trivial and they
kind of have to come up with some weak enforcement  of the continuity, where the random stochastic
rate is imposed on each constraint, continuity  constraint. So, this stochastic enforcement kind
of does not respect the physics. So, it is kind of  degrades the accuracy of the solution in general.
So, we have explored some existing method where  the combining ROM and domain decompensation and
there are some struggles in handling the wrong  interfaces. And the root cause of this struggle
is that unlike the polynomial analytic basis,  this POD or any other data driven basis does
not necessarily care for the interface. So,  the continuity or the smoothness is not really
guaranteed and the existing method circumvents  this by employing the separate interface spaces,
but they have their respective limitations. They  are either limited to a linear system or they have
to employ an arbitrary weak enforcement that  kind of does not respect the physics. And so,
this is what motivated us to use  this discontinuous Galerkin domain
decomposition. The POD basis does not guarantee  the continuity or the smoothness at the interface,
but DG basis does not have to match at the  element interfaces, and the discontinuity
or the non-smoothness they're allowed at the  interface. But by adding a penalty term like
such discontinuity can be controlled under the  desired numerical error convergent, which is
converging with a mesh refinement. And so, the  theory for this DG method has been really well

segments.text: Today we have Brian Young. And I don't know if you remember him. I think you gave us a talk about a year ago also in the MFEM workshop. Yes. We're very happy to have you here. Brian is an expert in electromagnetics, and digital signal integrated antenna design among others. Now, I believe you're retired, right? But you have worked in many places. Yeah. So I work full time now I just don't get paid. Okay, and today, you're going to talk about full wave electronic simulator for frequency domain S parameter calculations. Okay. We're very happy to have you here. Take it away. Okay, thank you. So, I have a kind of a standard agenda, go through the motivation for this work, features, S parameters, a little bit of background there, then the construction of the 3d simulator, how I've implemented adaptive mesh refinement, and then a number of examples, in discussion, a few comments on regression suite and conclusion. So the motivation for this work is that I'm not aware of any low cost or free frequency domain S parameter electromagnetic simulator. And because of that, there's very limited ability for an individual to explore ideas at home, or to work on continuing education. So the target audience is basically anyone who would like to be able to do 3d electromagnetic simulators and produce S parameters to try to come up with new things or self-educate or even say small startups that can't afford the very high cost of the commercial simulators. So as far as feasibility goes, I'm a one person effort. So you have to leverage existing open source projects. So to produce a 3d electromagnetic simulator, here's what I'm doing. I'm using free CAD for the CAD, Gmsh for meshing, MFEM for the finite element, and then visualization with ParaView. And that's essentially a simulator right there. So all you need to do is just glue it all together, which is quite a bit of work but not nearly as much, I think, as putting together any of the pieces that are required to pull together a full scale simulator. So the features I'm targeting is a full wave time harmonic 3d electromagnetic simulator that computes the electric and magnetic fields. And then from those fields extract S parameters between 2d ports on the surface of the 3d space. Courtesy of MFEM it supports high order arbitrary higher order elements, courtesy of MFEM, PETSc, SLEPc and some custom code also parallel processing via MPI. And then I'm also leveraging MFEM's adaptive mesh ability to do adaptive mesh refinement. So far, the one added feature that I need to add, one feature I need to add before releasing it is to add the impedance boundary condition, which I just left off, because I didn't want to mess with it to start off with, because there's so many things that have to be pulled together to get it started. So S parameters, in case you're not familiar with them, that's short for scattering parameters. It links the incident and reflected waves at the ports of a 3d volume. And for my experience in engineering across a number of companies and technical fields, is S parameters just dominate, frequency domain S parameters, that's just what's used to bring electromagnetic simulations into circuit simulations and for performance analyses. So for a practical simulator, in my opinion, that's just a must have requirement. So that's why the focus on this electromagnetic simulator is the primary output is targeting S parameters. Okay, so, a quick background one slide background on S parameters. If you have a 3d black box with N ports at each port, you'll have an incident wave and then some fraction of that wave will bounce back or some energy will come out from energy driven into another port. So, the convention in S parameters is the incident wave is A the reflected wave is B, if you have in ports, then you can relate the outputs to the inputs via the S parameter matrix. So, the target action then analysis is to get the 3d solution so that you can drive it with drive the space with incident waves, get the reflected waves, and then produce the S parameter matrix which is the output. So, the basic process is to find the ports which would be 2d flat surfaces on a 3d space, they have to be flat because the assumption is that the energy coming into the into the 3d space is from a transmission line, or waveguide, meaning that there's no dependence, the only dependence in the field is in the Z direction. So it has to be flat. Solve one column at a time by driving port I. And then if you don't, if you terminate all the other ports, then the reflected energy for I is not equal to the driven port, and those are zero because there's no energy coming in so you can dry port I get all the energy coming out of the other ports. And then you can pick off this parameter matrix one column at a time. So you have to repeat the simulation N times to fill out the full matrix. Once you've done that, you can then output the results in a Touchstone file format, which is what all the circuit simulators pull in. Results, viewers plotters, everything depends on Touchstone files. Okay, so this is a little bit more about the setup. Suppose you have a 3d space, you define the 2d ports on at each place where you want to drive energy and take energy out. The simulator uses MFEM’s ParSubMesh functionality to extract the 2d meshes on each of the 2d meshes at each port. The electromatic simulation is solved for the 2d simulation assuming it's a transmission line, using OpenParEM2D, which is what I presented at the workshop two workshops ago, then the 2d set field solution is applied to the 3d space, which forces the fields to take the 2d field solution. And then an absorbing boundary condition is applied to the other ports. So that gives you a unique setup that you can install the 3d electromagnetic simulation. And then you just cycle through and repeat that for all the ports. And when you're done, you can extract the S parameters. So moving on to the 3d finite element setup. The simulator uses the weak form of the wave equation. So this is basically exactly what everybody else does. So there's nothing innovative here. And MFEM is unique, is very well set up to solve this equation. With the one exception we'll talk about which makes it a little more interesting. So, the first term can be solved with the core curl integrator, second term with the vector FE mass integrator. The third term is this is the surface term. And that's where you need to apply boundary conditions and that's where the ports are. So you have to integrate bringing the ports from the surface term. So the surface term can be broken into the N ports. And then everything else. The surface is the surface that's not ports right now. Can be perfect electric conductor, which is easy to apply directly in the matrix by manipulating the DOFs and then there's the N ports which have to be considered. So copying the input the port setup, the surface for the ports the others, the part with the DOF manipulation. And then there's the part that has the N-crossed curl of E. And that term is not directly supported in MFEM. So that's where a little bit more work has to be applied to solve what needs to be solved using MFEM. And the way I'm handling that is similar, very similar to what's done in the literature, where you apply a vector identity to break the electric field into the tangential and normal components. And then to the derivative term, because you're making the assumption that the field at the ports is coming from a transmission line, the derivative with respect to the direction you're traveling, is known because it's just the propagation constant. So that's just written out of here on the right where the derivative because of the known dependence in the direction propagation, Z to the minus gamma, and you can take the derivative, and so you have one term out of this is just gamma times the tangential electric field, and that can be implemented with the vector Fv mass integrator. So that term is easy to take care of. The next term is the gradient is a gradient term of the normal component. And that operation is not supported in MFEM for Nedelec elements, because it includes a normal component on the boundary, but Nedelec elements don't have the normals on the boundaries. So what I'm choosing to do is to just neglect this term. And I have a whole slide next to talk about what happens when you neglect this term.
