segments.text: All right, so it's my pleasure to introduce  Ben Southworth today. Ben spent a lot of
time at Livermore, I remember when he was  a student here, and now he's at Los Alamos,
has been there for a while, doing a lot of  interesting work in many areas that intersect
MFEM and the type of discretizations we're  interested in. And today, he's going to talk
about discretization and solvers for anisotropic  problems, if I remember correctly, Ben thanks
for coming. It's a real pleasure to host you.  Please share and take it away. Thanks, Tzanio,
We’re ready. So I'm at Los Alamos National  Lab in T five and as Tzanio mentioned worked
in a lot of different areas. My background is  largely linear/nonlinear solvers. And lately,
I've been getting into time integration for  coupled systems and things like that. So I'm gonna
talk about discretizations and algebraic multigrid  solvers for extremely anisotropic diffusion,
in the context of magnetic confinement fusion.  And these discretizations and solvers are kind
of constructed using principles from hyperbolic  operators. And so this is joint work with Golo
Wimmer who's a young staff scientist here in  T five, also in Xianzhu Tang, who's much more
senior and works on magnetic confinement  fusion. And then Tom Gregory was a summer
student that did some of the results with us. And  so I just also want to highlight that, as I said,
I'm more of a solver person, and then a finite  element person, I'm a user of finite elements,
not a genius of finite elements or constructor new  things. And so I have to give a lot of credit to
Golo for taking kind of this vision I had of a way  to approach the solvers and work back and forth to
facilitate solvers and discretizations that are  compatible. And this is, to me, a super important
area of research for hard physics that doesn't get  enough attention. And that's getting compatible
solver and discretization, where you get the  accuracy you need. And it's also still tractable,
for fast, linear/nonlinear solvers. And it  can be hard to do that you can have a really
good discretization. And it's not uncommon for  those discretizations to also then be extremely
difficult to solve using conventional methods.  Okay, so this is the outline, I'm going to
provide a little bit of background on the problem,  anisotropic diffusion and different formulations
of it. And higher perspective on how we motivated  this use of hyperbolic operators. And then I'm
going to talk about the spatial discretization,  and the DG context, the CG context, and then just
some structure preservation comments on both types  of discretization. And I'll talk about accuracy
here. And then I'll move into the linear solvers  part. And this is a little bit backwards from how
we did the research, the original idea came from  the solver perspective, knowing the DG elements,
then we come back to solvers. And now we're  working on CG elements. And, and so I reorganized
to try to make it a little easier to follow. Okay,  so, anisotropic diffusion, most people know what
this is, we have the evolution of temperature  and plasma, forget the heat flux for now,
because we're in second order form, some forcing  term. And so here's our operator. And the way to
write it here is we have split the gradients into  cap parallel and cap perp. And so cap parallel
will be parallel with magnetic field lines. So  heat conduction following along magnetic fields,
and the cap perp was going to be orthogonal to the  magnetic field lines. And right, and so what will
be here is a normalized direction of magnetic  fields. And so this is a common way to write it
in second order form. It turns out when you have  extreme anisotropy, this is also not a good way
to write it. It's not good from the discretization  perspective when you get into the really extreme
anisotropy ratios. So another, there's many  different ways to skin the PDE as you could say,
or just to formulate it right. I mean, you have to  go back to the original problem and say, How are
we going to write it out? And so another way that  people use is to introduce a heat flux, right. So
you have the first order formulation of your  diffusion equation and you write in divergence
form your heat flux, and then we have this  forcing, then here's your flux and this is where
the anisotropy comes in. Again, same grad parallel  and grad purpose before. This is common. and still
not quite we're going to use here we're going to  use something similar and what we call Oh, sorry.
One more slide here, I forgot. When I say extreme  anisotropy in the context of magnetic confinement
fusion, it's really big. It's so the ratio is  like 10 to the 9th, 10 to the 10th In terms of the
ratio of conductivities in the direction of the  field versus orthogonal. And so what's interesting
about this problem when it gets this high in  anisotropy, is that the equation is parabolic
in nature, I mean, we're, if you're steady, it's  elliptic. But if you have a non-grid aligned
magnetic field, it's really hard from both from an  accuracy and the implicit solve perspective. And
that's kind of where this project came from, is  well. How do we solve this and, and my background
is in, again, algebraic multigrid, and I've worked  on AMG solvers for anisotropic diffusion. And I
thought we had pretty decent ones. And then I  worked, started working with fusion and said,
Okay, you know, give me some sample problems,  I can try set up a solver for it. It turns out,
there's little bit of a gap between what we do  in the solver literature and what they really
want to solve in their in their fusion problems.  And what we thought worked well did not work well
when we had a real problem. So we're going to use  for actual formulation is a directional gradient
formulation. So it's still effectively first  order form. And we still have this heat flux.
But what we do is we separate our conductivities  into an anisotropic conductivity. So this Kappa
Delta here, and then the anisotropic conductivity  is everything that's left. And so if Kappa Delta
is zero, then the diffusion is isotropic, and  for Kappa Delta much bigger than kappa perp,
then it ends up being predominantly anisotropic.  And so then instead of using the heat flux as an
auxiliary variable, we actually use a directional  gradient. So this B dot grad T, a scale by the by
the anisotropic conductivity, this ends up being  our auxiliary variable. And so then this is the
kind of continuous form of the equations, we have  a first order form for the anisotropic components.
So here and here, and then we have a second order  form for the isotropic diffusion. And this is kind
of separating off the difficult part from the  part that we know how to solve, everybody can
solve isotropic diffusion from a discretization  and solver perspective. And so to kind of get into
the motivation of where this all came from, if  you write out this formulation in a block operator
form, so forget your discretization for now,  just keep the strong far differential operators,
we have our temperature, we have our auxiliary  variable. And up here we are time gradient and
temperature and our isotropic diffusion. And  then our off diagonal operators end up being the
directional gradients, that's how we formulated  with this coupling, sorry, this coupling between
them. And in a finite element case, this would be  a mass matrix. And so if we look at this and say,
Okay, let's take a limit, right, let's take  the anisotropic limit, because when we get
to 10 to the nine ratios, where we're almost  zero isotropic diffusion anyway. And let's say
we skip the time curves. So we're just going full  steady state, fully anisotropic diffusion. If we,
write it out like that, and rearrange the system,  it's equivalent to this form here. And so instead
of a diffusion system, now, what we really  have is two coupled hyperbolic operators,
directional gradients in the direction magnetic  fields coupled with this mass matrix. And that's
this limiting asymptotic of our system. It's  in the case of steady and I know diffusion in
the isotropic setting. And so this is kind of my  original vision is, I tried some solvers on the
anisotropic problem, classical AMG formulations,  things like that, with, you know, tailored AMG
methods for anisotropic diffusion, and it just  did not work. It just did not work. And so I said,
Well, what if we rewrite the system and  pose it in terms of hyperbolic operators,
and focus on solving that, because the other big  background that I have is I worked a lot on AMG
methods for transport. And that's a big focus of  my thesis and the research thereafter. And so if
we rearrange the system, and think about it like  this, we can apply this specific AMG solver I have
to these equations. It's very fast and effective,  and with the right discretization context,
and then we don't have to worry about the  anisotropy. Instead, we kind of solve these
advection operators with separate techniques. And  so that's kind of the big picture in this regime
of extreme anisotropy, I am kind of claiming  that we should really treat this parabolic
equation as a system of couple of hyperbolic  operators rather than a parabolic operator.
And that's not a common thing to do parabolic  equations and elliptic equations have so many
nice properties. It's not necessarily intuitive to  move away from that into the regime of hyperbolic
operators which have zero nice properties. But  it actually can be very useful in this regard.
Okay, so that's kind of big picture now I’m going  to talk about the spatial discretization. And we
start with discontinuous Galerkin finite elements.  So most people here are probably familiar with the
standard upwind DG discretization of transport.  And so that's what we used to discretize our
directional gradient here. So this is our weak  form for our transport in one direction, and we
have our element integral and then our facet  integral here. Again, when we used to capital
gamma to define that the set of all interior  facets, we have upwinding, using this twiddle
here, and then we have our outflow boundary  condition for this direction of transport, we
have a standard jump notation. And the reason we  did this originally, again, this is kind of trying
to make compatible solvers and discretizations  is we had this idea, okay, let's try to solve the
transport operators. And, like many solvers,  air, which is what I'm going to use now talk
about later, is finicky, it doesn't work for any  advection discretization, it really works really
well for upwind stabilized discretizations. And so  I told Golo, you know, we should try to treat this
transport term using an upwind discretization  because that's what we can solve. And so the
full weak form we have two transport operators,  alright, one on each off diagonal of our coupled
two by two system. And there's one nuance here  in that when we pose it as a transport operator,
we need transport boundary condition, right, if  we just consider discretizing the first order
gradient without a time derivative, if we can’t  impose boundary conditions on the whole domain,
and so we need an inflow boundary condition. And  for one of the transport operators, this is fine,
it ends up being naturally extends from the  boundary conditions of your temperature. For
the other one, we introduced this zeta in here,  which is we kind of assumed to be known. And whole
purpose of this, again, is if we know the inflow  boundary conditions, and this ensures that these
operators are invertible. If we want to apply  algebraic multigrid to the advection equations,
it needs to be invertible. At least for now. We'll  talk more about that later. And so there's two
ways we can do this. One of them is simple, we  just iterate within a Picard iteration implicit
solve until we have this inflow boundary condition  equal to the solution, zeta H. And here, we just
want to comment right now we're focusing on a  linear formulation of the problem. But really,
in anything practical this is going to be a full  nonlinear equation, and T where the diffusion
coefficients really depend on temperature. And  so within the nonlinear iteration for T, we're
like 99% sure that this right here is less stiff  and easier to resolve than the actual temperature
nonlinearity. And so we think that we're going  to get this for free when we go nonlinear.
In the meantime, we're doing it in kind of an  implicit explicit approach where we just treat the
auxiliary inflow explicitly. And interestingly,  we found this to be very slowly in time, it’s non
stiff, and we haven't had any problems with that  kind of implicit explicit treatment. So we can
include it in an outer iteration, if we want to  but right now, we don't do that. And so these are
our two transport operators. And the full weak  form of our directional gradient formulation,
and the mix DG formulation is given here, so we  have our time derivative, we have our transport
operator in the primary variable and temperature,  IP, this just stands for a typical interior
penalty, discontinuous Galerkin discretization  of the isotropic component of diffusion. Here
we have a boundary integral and forcing term.  And we have our auxiliary equation here with
our other transport operators. And so again, here  we choose the order of our DG spaces to be equal,
to ensure square and vertical diagonal blocks,  right, if we choose different order elements
that are off diagonal in the mix system end up  being non square and not vertical. So this is
the weak form. And I'm gonna show that it works.  So we formulated a kind of MHD test problem. It's
motivated by problems in magnetohydrodynamics. But  we want to get rid of all the other physics for
now and really just focus on the discretization  solver of the diffusion. So we define a 3d domain
that's periodic in Z, kind of roughly simulating  the tokamak situation, you would get magnetic
confinement fusion. And we start with this  initial temperature here, it's effectively a
manufactured solution. And we choose our magnetic  field to align with the contours of T naught and
be constant in the Z. And so this is just how you  do that. And what this does is ensures that the 2d
curl of your initial temperature is given by our  B field. And so what we do is we can add a counter
force in term in the manufactured solutions, to  ensure that the actual time the continuous time
evolution of this equation is really a steady  state test case. And so in doing that we can
measure the discretization error over time,  and how it accumulates relative to some known
solution that we should be at. And so this is  how we measure the error. And so we compare
with three different systems, we have a CG primal  system, that's continuous Galerkin second order
elements. In the typical second order formulation  for the problem, we do the same with a DG primal
system. And so this has been used recently,  with some papers using MFEM and also, Chris
Vogel and Milan and Ilan of AMR. Using this kind  of discretization. And then we use the mixed CG
formulation. So this was the original directional  gradient formulation in the literature,
as far as we know, this was maybe 10 years ago or  something, a paper Gunter et al. proposed using
the directional gradient formulation, but they do  not use any transport discretization technique.
So they just do a mixed form. And then just kind  of standard CG and DG basis functions and mixed
formulations to formulate the system. And so use  CG two and DG one in the auxiliary space. Okay,
and so here are the accuracy and results  for our DG discretization applied to this
kind of manufacturer solution test problem. And  we have is a relative L two error and the three
plots correspond to the anisotropy ratio.  So on the left, we have 10 to the three,
this is not so bad, it's not realistic in the in  the magnetic confinement fusion test case but this
is kind of what I thought might be a realistic  problem before I got into the fusion problem. So I
had AMG solvers that could work well on this. And  we see that the accuracy also for discretization
works well. Then we go to 10 to the six and 10 to  the nine. And that's where we were very pleasantly
surprised to find not only does the stabilization  and upwinding make sense and work well for the
solvers, it actually helps substantially for the  discretizations. And so in this far right plot,
we're at 10 to the nine which is again, the kind  of ratios we expect to see, in practice, we're
getting three orders of magnitude more accurate  solutions using oh my gosh, what happened, sorry,
three orders of magnitude more accurate solution  using the new mixed DG scheme than any of these
other three finite element formulations. And, and  these aren't even converging in proper order. Yet,
as you continue to refine, I expect they  eventually well, they're starting to find
that convergence, but it's taking quite a while  to get there. Okay, and that’s DG, and we have a
paper on that one online right now. And the  paper discusses the DG element formulation,
and then the initial solver framework too. But  before we get into solvers, I'm now going to
talk about continuous elements, which is what we  started working on this fall. And so this is kind
of ongoing work. But the idea is basic, it's  that well, we have this new DG discretization,
that not only worked for the solvers, but actually  provided very good accuracy. And we use a similar
formulation in the continuous element case. And  so, here for easy notation, I just dropped the
isotropic component, it's exactly the same as DG  we use kind of standard continuous Galerkin finite
element discretization of the isotropic part of  the operator in the primary variable equation
here. So we let VT be our eighth order continuous  Galerkin space and then these boundary conditions
spaces and auxiliary space. And so here, this  is our weak form, and we drop the isotropic
components, we have these two transport operators  directional v dot grad eta, and b dot grad T
and the auxiliary equation. And then here in  principle, you can choose whatever auxiliary
space you want, it can be CG or DG with different  orders. Similar to DG for the purposes of focusing
on the advection solver, we choose the auxiliary  space to equal that of the temperature space. And
that way we have square advective blocks that  in the case of open field lines are invertible.
And so transport stabilization, we discovered  that it works really well from the distribution
perspective for DG elements. So we're going to  try the same thing here. And the analog that
we're working with is using SUPG stabilization.  And so to do this, we define our velocity field S
as effectively the scaled the appropriately scaled  magnetic field direction. And we have the SUPG
stabilization parameter tau and we defined to SUPG  operators called the advective and the flux based
SUPG operator and they're similar, one is just the  tau is inside or outside of the of the gradient.
And so in the mix CG, stabilized discretization  in weak form is given right here. And a lot of it
looks like what you might expect. It's just like  the previous weak form where we've introduced our
stabilized operators. And then we now have this  boundary integral as well. But everything else is
kind of as you'd expect. And so a few comments  on that boundary integral appears because even
though eta vanishes along the Dirichlet boundary,  the SUPG modifications do not. So when we use the
stabilized operators, we need to add a boundary  integral to enforce that in the solution space,
we choose this averaged stabilization parameter  for tau. This is kind of taking two different
commonly used stabilizations. So one of them's the  more or less speed divided by the mesh spacing.
And the other is scaling of the time derivative  and combine the both, take the inverse. And so I
should say I introduced those two specific forms  of our SUPG operators, our advective in our flux
based SUPG. These were chosen very particularly  for structure preservation and consistency.
So I'll get to that in the last slide. But we  had a few structural properties that we wanted
to preserve in our discretization. And so we  started there. And then in doing the derivations,
we kind of worked out exactly what SF and SA  need to be in the weak formulation to satisfy
these properties. And then finally, in practice,  we use weak boundary conditions for the continuous
Galerkin formulation. And this is nonstandard.  Typically, if you use CG, then you strong
boundary conditions. But if you remember that,  when we're doing this, we're a big part of the
algorithm is swapping the rows of the assembled  system so that in the mix formulation, the mixed
operators are actually on the diagonal. And at  least in Firedrake, I know I'm sorry, we're using
Firedrake for this testing, but that's where Golo  was working at the time, and it was easiest for
him to implement things. It was nontrivial. And  by that, I mean, we had no idea how to form the
correct block row Swap System was strong boundary  conditions, because as nice as UFL language is for
finite elements to get in and modify the matrices  and the resulting system is a pain. So we will be
moving to MFEM at some point in the foreseeable  future. And perhaps this will be easier to do
in MFEM. Okay. And so
again, we have a new test case here,  it's a little bit different. Here,
we have what we call a magnetic surface test  case. So in magnetic confinement fusion, plasma
gets trapped in these series of concentric torii  going around. And so what we do is we unfold all
these into a 2d surface and make a periodic and  sorry not, yeah, periodic, we pretty much unfold
it and we use a rational winding number. If you're  a plasma physicist, you have a good idea what this
is. Don't ask me for a good explanation because I  don't have one. Except for that, if it's rational,
the heat stays along certain structures. If  it's irrational, eventually it will fill up
the whole domain. So irrational winding number  and an initial temperature perturbation. And we
watch how it spreads on the surface. And so here  we choose, actually zero isotropic diffusion,
and then everything's in the anisotropic  direction. And so this is in some sense harder
and easier. The problem itself is easier than the  previous one. But we stay in the fully anisotropic
regime. And we integrate out to one Alfven time.  And so again, here's the accuracy on the quads,
the purple triangles, that's q2 So we just mean  here, standard second order CG discretization
applied to the second order operator. The red  triangles are mixed. That's the Gunter et al.
CG two discontinuous Galerkin one and the green  is our new mixed stabilized CG two discretization.
And so our quads we do well we're you know, about  a little over an order of magnitude smaller error
than these schemes, and overall it looks really  good. What's interesting is it looks a lot better
with triangles. We I'm not sure why these existing  schemes struggle on triangles, but they do. They
infer quads a lot and our new scheme is pretty  much indifferent. From a computation perspective.

cheaper anyway. So yeah, so here we're getting  at this point, not quite two orders of magnitude
but pretty close a better error using our new  discretization than existing methods in the
literature. Okay, yeah, lots of time. Okay,  so the last part on the discretizations is
to talk about structure preservation a little  bit. So this Golo’s background is in structure
preserving finite elements specifically in terms  of atmospheric sciences and geosciences. But
it's good to think about these things. And it's  been nice to talk to him about. So consistency,
